The entire world—that is, the whole universe appearing as something external—[arises] from the pure principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*) which constitutes the universal aggregate (*samaṣṭi*). For indeed, the entire world has originated from the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) himself. In this context, it should be understood that the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) form of the mind serves as the point of comparison (*upamāna*), because the universal form of the mind is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
In this corner of Jambudvīpa, in the region named Bhārata, he created people who were overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease.
Having made the people—the human race—consist of both the *prajāpatis* who were his sons and the common folk.

It distinguishes the people whose limbs are dejected by the notions of existence and non-existence, who are intent on creation and destruction; yet it is the supreme means of nourishment for the various classes of beings in this creation.
Of the classes of beings such as the gods and others; it causes nourishment, bringing satisfaction by means of sacrificial offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Seeing the constant suffering of those people, the Lord, the creator of all worlds, was moved by compassion, just as a father is by the suffering of his son.
The Lord of those people—of the human race—is Brahmā and the principle of the pure mind (*śuddhamanastattva*). Compassion (*karuṇā*) means mercy.
And here, the compassion of the pure mind should be understood as entering the consciousness of the poet who is creating the memory being produced; enough with this disclosure of the secret.
"Now, what did he do after that? To this, [the author] says:
"What end of suffering could there be for these wretched ones, whose lives are forfeit? Thinking thus with one-pointed concentration for a moment, the Lord of Beings reflected. (MU 2.10.17)
Of those whose hopes are destroyed, who have perished; of those whose life-span is ended, who are subject to decay; "the end" means the final limit.
Having thus reflected,
the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, brought his contemplation to an end and once again created austerity, righteousness, charity, truth, and indeed the sacred fords.
"He himself created" means that he perceived [the contents] as duties toward people once the treatises on law (smṛti-śāstra) had been composed.
Having created this, the divine creator of beings reflected again: "By this alone, there shall be no end to the suffering of men," he thought himself.
This is clear.
Furthermore, suspecting that one might ask by what means the end of all suffering for men will come about, he reflects:
"Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss, by which a person is neither born nor dies; it is obtained through knowledge alone."

Anticipating the question, "By what means might that nirvāṇa be attained?", he reflects: "From knowledge. That [is] nirvāṇa; it is obtained from knowledge alone—that is, from the knowledge of the reality of the supreme Self—*and not* from asceticism (*tapas*) and the like.
He himself establishes the propriety of employing the word "only" [in the phrase "knowledge alone"]:
"For indeed, knowledge alone is the means for a living being to cross over saṃsāra; austerity, charity, and likewise pilgrimage are proclaimed as inferior means. (MU 2.10.21)
The minor means is the intermediate means.
Then, anticipating the doubt as to how knowledge will be established for people, he reflects:
"Therefore, for the sake of this great-souled person's liberation from suffering, I shall quickly reveal a fresh and youthful means."
This reflection, however, should be understood as occurring through the entry of the mental absorption (*cintāveśa*) directed toward the teacher who will impart the knowledge that is about to arise.
Having thus reflected and withdrawn his supreme contemplation, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, born from the lotus, formed a mental resolve and brought me into existence.

"Me"—that is, me, named Vasiṣṭha, who am the foremost among those teachers who have proclaimed the source of the arising of my own inconceivable [wisdom], and who am capable of producing knowledge in people like you by teaching the scripture known as the *Mokṣopāya*. The use of the word "with the mind" (*manasā*) is a grammatical construction similar to the expression "the head of Rāhu."
"Surely, by what material cause were you produced? To this he replied:
"O sinless one, having arisen from somewhere indeed very quickly, I appeared before that father as swiftly as one wave from another."

I was born from some indefinable material cause; thereafter, I quickly appeared—that is, arrived—in the presence of that father. From what was I born? Like a wave from a wave. Since, upon ultimate investigation, the birth of all things is invisible, it is here described as a birth in a general sense; enough with revealing this secret.
"What kind of person have you become, and what have you done? To this, the Lord replied:
"Carrying a water-pot, I was saluted and greeted by him who also carried a water-pot; holding a rosary, I was saluted by him who also held a rosary. (MU 2.10.25)
"Accompanied by a rosary" is an adverbial modifier for the preceding action; by this, his own meditative concentration is described.
Then, [the Lord asked: "What was said by him to you, and what was done? To this he replied:
"Having said to me, 'Come, my son,' he joined me with his hand upon the northern petal of his own lotus, like the cool-rayed moon to a white cloud."
Here, it is stated by way of a turn of phrase that "the touch of a pure mind has arisen in me."
Clad in a deer skin, with his own garment being a deer skin, my father Brahmā spoke to me, as a swan speaks to a crane.
"Mām" means "me," namely the one called Vasiṣṭha; and here, the intermediate reference [to the word] "vacanam" (the statement) should be understood.
"What did he say? To this he replied:
"O son, for a mere moment your mind, as fickle as a monkey, was overcome by ignorance, just as the hare [mark] enters the moon."
Indeed, it is solely by virtue of the pure mind abiding in its internal state that ignorance and knowledge arise for all beings; by this, his own state of being a knower is first illuminated.
He concludes the words of Brahmā:
"Thus, having been cursed by him immediately after my reflection, I, O twice-born one, forgot my entire stainless true nature."
"I am a twice-born Brāhmaṇa named Vasiṣṭha; I have forgotten my own true nature"—this is the connection [of the words].
Then, having fallen into a state of dejection and remaining with an unawakened mind, I was consumed by suffering and grief, like a lowly person born into the world.
By means of non-awakening, which is devoid of certainty.
"How has this affliction called 'saṃsāra' come to be?"—thus he reflected within himself and remained silent.
The connection is that he thought, "I [am]. By this, it is indicated that immediately after his state of ignorance, the manifestation of his own dispassion occurred.
Then my father said to me: "Son, why are you sorrowful? Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be forever happy."
Then he spoke; by this it was indicated that immediately after detachment, my inclination toward knowledge arose.
"Surely, what did you do after that? To this he replied:
"Then, having been questioned by me while seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, [taught] the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra."
By this, it is indicated that the investigation was conducted by me myself.
"Surely you asked him this, and what did he say? To this he replied:
"O Lord, how has this great suffering of saṃsāra come to be? And how is it exhausted for a living being?"—this was what I asked when he had been questioned by me.
That knowledge has been declared to be most abundant, by knowing which it is the supreme purifier; indeed, I stand as if even superior to my father.

The state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*) attained by transcending the principle of the pure mind (*śuddhamanastattva*) should be understood as the superiority of the Father (*pituḥ*). By this, its self-established nature (*svataḥsiddhatvam*) is stated. For there are three kinds of perfected ones (*siddhāḥ*), each possessing a progressive excellence: from the teacher (*gurutaḥ*), from scripture (*śāstrataḥ*), and from oneself (*svataḥ*).

Then the Creator of the world, the speaker and the cause of all things, spoke to me, who had realized what is to be known and was established in my own true nature: The Creator of the world, the speaker and the cause of all things, spoke to me, who had realized what is to be known and was established in my own true nature.
"This has manifested within me"—this is the internal intention.
"What did he say? To this he replied:
"Having reduced him to a state of ignorance through a curse, you were made by me an inquirer, so that the essence of knowledge might be attained by all people."
The meaning is that it occurred to me: "This very ignorance has manifested within me."
What did he say again? To this he replied:
"Now that the curse has been pacified, you have attained supreme awakening; you stand as one with the Self, like gold [separated] from gold. (MU 2.10.38)
The meaning is that even the thought "now I have become a knower" has flashed through my mind.
Furthermore, what did he say after that? To this he replied:
"O virtuous one, go now for the sake of favoring the worlds to Bhārata-varṣa, the great seat situated within Jambūdvīpa."
This is clear.
In that regard, O son, those of great intelligence who are devoted to the section on ritual action should be instructed by you, step by step, according to the sequence of the ritual action section.
This is clear.
O virtuous one, those whose minds are detached, who possess great wisdom, and who are free from passion—these should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss.

Therefore, I shall provide instruction through the door of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) for those devoid of dispassion, but through the door of the knowledge section (*jñānakāṇḍa*) for those who are dispassionate; this is what has flashed across my mind. Otherwise, I would not even engage in your instruction—this is the underlying sense.
He concludes the words of Brahmā:
"Thus commissioned by my father, the lotus-born one, I remain here, O Rāghava, as long as the succession of living beings endures."

The phrase "the succession of beings" (*bhūtaparaṃparā*) has been stated either as a general reference to the knowledge of beings possessed by teachers, or on account of his own long life; however, the external object has not been explicitly stated at every step for the sake of clarity.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever here that remains to be done by me; thus, with the conceit 'I am established on the earth,' I perform my duties with a disposition that is utterly tranquil, as if with a mind perpetually asleep, and yet I do nothing at all."

Indeed, this is certain: for me, belonging to the lineage of all the wise known as Vasiṣṭha, there is nothing whatsoever left to be done in this world, because I have accomplished all that was to be done through the attainment of the reality of the Supreme Self. Nevertheless, I remain established here upon the earth. In what manner? I must certainly remain here; I must remain in accordance with the dictates of destiny.

"Thus-minded" means one whose mind is thus intent, whose mind is thus fixed, up to the point of being one whose mind is thus resolved. "By me" refers to one who acts with a disposition that is perfectly tranquil—that is, free from the agitation consisting of the pursuit of gain or loss. "I perform" both the "transcendent task," which is action for the sake of maintaining the body's livelihood, and the "obligatory task," which is action performed to avoid the fault of transgression (*pratyavāya*). By what kind of disposition? Like that intellect which is perpetually asleep—as if by that which is utterly tranquil.
The meaning is this: nevertheless, because of the experience of the certainty that "I do not do even the slightest thing" and "I am not the agent," [there is no action].
Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the tenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
With the desire to conclude what was stated regarding the previous creation, he makes this reference:
"All this has been told to you—the descent of knowledge upon earth, as well as my own endeavor, fashioned by the Lotus-born One."

His own endeavor, his personal activity, was fashioned and manifested by the lotus-born Brahmā through the principle of the pure mind (*śuddhamanastattva*). The sense is that in this very manner, knowledge has descended here [into this world].
O sinless one, today my heart is intensely eager to hear this supreme knowledge, owing to the ripening of my great merit.
That was spoken by Brahmā.
Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Brahmin, how did the intellect of the Supreme Lord, the Parameṣṭhin, proceed toward the descent of knowledge in the world immediately after the creation?"
"How" means "for what purpose. //MT_2,11.3//
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks further:
Within the supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself is born by the power of his own nature, eternally consisting of vibration, like a wave in the ocean.
In the supreme, most excellent nature of pure consciousness alone, that which consists of vibration is that which consists of the limited reflective awareness of "I."
Having thus created this extended creation, the Supreme Lord beheld all the destinies of that creation, situated in the past, the present, and the future.
He saw; the words "with the eye of knowledge" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
When the time for the performance of ritual acts belonging to the Kṛta age and the others had come to an end, the Lord, perceiving the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion.
The meaning is: "delusion that is yet to come."
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge, dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world.
Having joined me—who am known as Vasiṣṭha—with knowledge, that is, with the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
Just as I have been dispatched by him, so too have many other great seers, headed by Sanatkumāra and including Nārada and others.
By this, it is indicated that this very same method applies to those teachers who have been, and those who will be, in the future as well.
Through the sequence of ritual action and likewise through the sequence of gnosis, these [teachings] were proclaimed in order to uplift the world, which is bound by the great malady of the mind.

They were impelled, that is, they were sent forth. For what purpose? To uplift the world through the sequence of ritual action and the sequence of knowledge, according to the distinctions among those qualified [to receive them].
In what state is the world? The mind itself is the "great delusion" (mahāmaya), which is a great disease; by that, the world is "stretched out," meaning it is bound.

Then, in ancient times, when the Kṛta Yuga had waned, and the pure sequence of ritual action had gradually diminished upon the earth, the great seers appointed kings according to the division of separate regions for the purpose of establishing the system of ritual action and for the regulation of social boundaries.
This is clear.
Furthermore, many treatises on memory (smṛti) and treatises on sacrifice (yajña) have been composed and proclaimed on this earth for the sake of achieving dharma, pleasure, and wealth.

They were fabricated and composed by the great seers (*maharṣi*); this is the ellipsis. The sense is that their instruction was not heard by the world. The word *atha* (now/then) is to be connected with the following verse.
While this wheel of time continues to turn, and while that sequence has thus dissolved, people remain intent on eating every day and devoted to the acquisition of rice.
Conflicts have arisen among kings for the sake of sense objects, and living beings on earth have come to be subjected to punishment in great numbers.

"Dvandvāni" means dual combats. "For the sake of territory" means for the sake of land. "Punishability" (daṇḍyatām) means being fit for punishment; the sense is that this results from committing sins such as adultery with another's wife.
Then, gradually becoming incapable of protecting the earth without war, the kings, along with their subjects, fell into a state of wretchedness.
This is clear.
In order to dispel their dejection and for the sake of the correct process of creation, great visions of knowledge were then proclaimed by us and others.
Of those kings.
This is the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā); it was first described among kings, and subsequently spread throughout the world, wherefore it is called the "royal science" (rājavidyā).
The intention is that because it is designated by the term "royal science" (*rājavidyā*) in the *Gītā* and other texts through such passages as "the royal science, the royal secret," and so forth.

"O Rāghava, having understood this supreme treatise on the inner self—the royal science and the royal secret—kings have attained the highest state beyond suffering. "The royal secret" is another name for the science of the inner self.
Now, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away, you, O Rāma, have been born today here on this earth from this Daśaratha.
This is clear.
And in your mind, O crusher of foes, there has arisen this pure, causeless, and beautiful dispassion toward that which is exceedingly dear to you.
"Signless" means without a sign such as the form of the loathsome and so forth.
"Surely, what excellence do I possess that my dispassion is without cause? To this he replies:
"O Rāma, for every fortunate and virtuous person who possesses discernment, dispassion arises preceded by a cause; it is of the nature of passion (rājasa). (MU 2.11.21)
This is clear.

But this unprecedented state that has arisen, which causes wonder among the virtuous— this dispassion of yours, which is without external cause, characterized by purity, and born from your own discernment— is truly marvelous.
This is clear.
Who indeed would not become dispassionate upon seeing the loathsome and the foul? But for the virtuous, supreme detachment arises solely from discernment.
The loathsome [object] is a substance that serves as the objective basis for the loathsome rasa.
Indeed, those great ones of vast wisdom, for whom detachment arises even without a sign, are the ones whose minds are stainless.
The meaning is that without a pure state of mind, dispassion characterized by the signless does not arise.
Indeed, by means of an intellect detached through the contemplation of the wonder of its own discernment, a living being shines like a youth adorned with a forest garland.
The wonder of one's own discernment—by the reflection upon that, and by being dispassionate, meaning free from attachment to external objects, but not dispassionate through loathing.
Those who, having discerned this structure of worldly existence through discrimination, attain dispassion—they alone are the supreme among men.
This is clear.
Having investigated this again and again by the power of one's own discernment, one must forcibly abandon this magical illusion, both external and internal.
This so-called saṃsāra is a magical illusion; it must be abandoned entirely and brought to the state of being an object of relinquishment.
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing the cemetery, misfortune, and wretchedness? That dispassion which arises spontaneously is the supreme good.
This is clear.
You possess unartificial dispassion and have attained full greatness; you are a fit vessel for the essence of knowledge, just as soft soil is for a seed.
This is clear.
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Protector, the Supreme Self, a virtuous intellect such as yours pursues discernment.
The intended meaning is that, however, no personal effort whatsoever is effective in this regard.
Through the sequence of ritual actions, through great austerity, through self-restraint, through charity, through pilgrimages to sacred fords, and through long-term discernment;

When evil deeds have come to an end and one engages in the investigation of the ultimate truth, the intellect of a living being proceeds by way of a chance occurrence, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence.

By the phrase "by way of a chance occurrence" (*kākatālīyayogena*), the laxity of the sequence of ritual actions and so forth is indicated. Through a chance occurrence, there arises the application of the intellect directed toward the investigation of the Supreme Self.

Nevertheless, the sequence of ritual actions and so forth must certainly be performed; for even that [action] serves as a means toward that [realization] to some small extent. And one should not become complacent in that alone, because there exists another primary means, such as the service of a true guru.
Enough.
People devoted to ritual action continue to revolve here like the turning of a wheel, as long as they do not behold the supreme state.

Those devoted to ritual action (kriyāparāḥ), regarding ritual action alone as the means, [seek] the supreme state, the exalted station called pure consciousness (cinmātra). "By means of the revolutions of the wheels" means that those devoted to ritual action are repeatedly engaged in such activity.
Having seen this cyclic existence as it truly is, and having abandoned the mind that is absorbed in it, they go to the supreme state like elephants freed from their tethering posts.

Having seen things as they truly are, having seen them exactly as they exist—[they attain] that which is composed of that [reality], which consists of saṃsāra; they go toward, they experience their own self as that supreme, transcendent reality of pure consciousness alone. O Rāma, this course of worldly existence is difficult and endless. Released from the body, the great thread [of bondage] does not perish without knowledge.

The path of saṃsāra is that stream of worldly existence whose endless efforts consist of the forms of both being and non-being; it is called the "Great Thread Released from the Body" (dehamuktā mahātantuḥ). Knowledge is the knowledge of the reality of pure consciousness alone (cinmātratattvajñāna).

O descendant of Raghu, it is by the very raft of the application of knowledge that those of great intelligence have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross, and not by any other means.
The method (yukti) which consists of knowledge is the means; that itself is the raft. By means of it...
Listen with an attentive mind to this method of knowledge, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, by means of this constant attentiveness.
The meaning is that you are unable to hear [this] without an attentive mind.
O blameless one, because the ways of suffering in the world involve endless turmoil, these burn within for a long time unless there is a remedy.
The reasoning known as knowledge; that is, reasoning.
O Raghava, by what means can the dualities of suffering—such as cold, wind, and heat—be endured even by the virtuous, unless there is the application of knowledge?
"By what other means? means by no means whatsoever. In this context, however, the consumption of black pepper by children and the elderly should be applied as an illustrative example.
Afflictions of grief fall upon the foolish man at every step and at their appointed time, consuming him just as a flame of fire burns straw.
Thoughts that bestow suffering are "thoughts of suffering"; they should be understood as having objects of enjoyment as their domain.
Mental anxieties do not burn the wise man who has realized true knowledge and possesses right vision, just as the flames of fire do not consume a forest during a year of heavy rains.

How was the wise one? He was one by whom the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*)—which is consciousness and has the nature of cognition (*vijñāna*)—was known and experienced. What were his mental anxieties (*ādhi*)? They were his reflections (*cintā*). How was the forest? It was one in which clouds (*abdāḥ*, i.e., rain-clouds) were raining.
Even when the desert wind of saṃsāra, which revolves with mental and physical afflictions, is turbulent, the knower of reality is not broken, like the wish-fulfilling tree.

In that which is agitated by the repeated recurrence and reversal of mental and physical afflictions—that is, in a state of agitation characterized by existence and non-existence—he is not broken; he does not fall under the sway of joy and sorrow. This should be understood as occurring when the desert wind of *saṃsāra* is turbulent.
Even the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) is not broken when the wind is turbulent.
Therefore, in order to know reality, only a wise person should diligently and with humility inquire of another who is wise, authoritative, and awakened in soul.

"Authoritative" means one who speaks according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Awakened" means known; he by whom the Self—the Supreme Self whose nature is pure consciousness—is known, is "one whose Self is awakened. "Endowed with affection" means accompanied by a request. The implication is that one other than such a person, when questioned, might say something quite contradictory.
The words of an authoritative person who has been questioned should be received with effort by one of noble mind, just as saffron is absorbed by fine cloth.
With effort and with careful attention.
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions a person who does not know reality and whose words are not to be accepted.
"Such a person" means one who does not know reality, that is to say, one who conceives of a self in the body and so forth.
There is no one more base than that person who, when questioned with effort by an authoritative speaker who knows the truth, does not carry out his word.
One who does not carry out the speech does not accomplish the meaning expressed by the words spoken.
Having first ascertained through the effect whether the speaker possesses knowledge of that matter or lacks it, the man who then poses a question is a person of great intelligence.
This is established by their actions, and not by mere words; for by mere words, many people present themselves as knowers of Brahman.
The child who asks a question without having first determined the speaker is an inferior inquirer; he is not a fit vessel for the great meaning.
A fool is one who is deluded like a child; [he is ignorant] of the great purpose, which is the supreme goal known as liberation.
When one possesses a blameless intellect capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows, a wise person should speak when questioned; not to one who is base and follows the nature of a beast.

To one who is wise and intelligent, by a teacher; to one who has asked—that is, who has made a subject the object of inquiry; to one who is blameless; and likewise to one whose intellect possesses the capacity for resolution—that is, the removal of mutual contradictions—regarding the meanings of the preceding and following parts of the discourse; to such an inquirer should one speak. However, to one who is base, and for that very reason like a beast due to his delusion, [one should not].
When the questioner is like a beast, one should not speak, because it would be in vain.

The wise in this world call that man the most foolish who speaks without having first considered whether the meaning he utters is consistent with authoritative sources and logically tenable for the questioner.

Because the questioner is more foolish, this [opponent] is the most foolish of all; for among many who inquire about the nature of birth, he is the most foolish. The sense is: what could even this fool, who is more ignorant than the questioner himself, possibly say?
O descendant of Raghu, you are an exceedingly great repository of virtues and a seeker of knowledge; I am capable of speaking, and this is the union of us two.
The connection (*yoga*) is a relationship between similar things: namely, that you are one who inquires about the receptacle of virtues, while I am one who speaks accordingly.
O you who are skilled in words and their meanings, whatever I say should be determined by you with effort as being this very reality, and held in your heart without wavering.
He describes the nature of the final determination: "This" refers to this subject matter spoken by the venerable Vasiṣṭha; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

At first, my word should be accepted as true simply out of devotion; thereafter, its truth will manifest of its own accord. Otherwise, at the very outset, by means of subtle investigations based on one's own conceptual constructions—
The sense is that not even the slightest thing will succeed for you.
"Now, if what you have said does not apply to me, then what should be done? To this he replies:
"You are great, you are dispassionate, and you are a knower of reality regarding the condition of living beings; thus the truth takes root within you, just as saffron water clings to a cloth."
Since you are great and not base— for a base person is agitated even by a slight thing due to their baseness—

and since you are dispassionate toward worldly objects, for otherwise you would lack the fitness of one whose intellect is obsessed with material things; likewise, you are skilled and proficient in the maintenance and arrangement of the populace, for otherwise, following that analogy...
The instruction previously mentioned does not take root in you; therefore, the ultimate reality (paramārthatattva) spoken by me takes root in you.
How so? Like saffron water; the meaning is that it takes root in you just as that [saffron water] adheres to a garment.
Your wisdom, which is supremely attentive and discerns the ultimate truth, enters into the object like the light of the sun into the midst of water.

Regarding what was said: that very attention which is yours is "supreme" (paramam), meaning it is excellent as an object of apprehension; such [is your intellect]. Likewise, your discerning wisdom (prajñā) enters into the meaning—the meaning of my words—of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), which is the internal meaning of the statements I have uttered.
It "enters" (viśati) in the sense of being present nearby. Here he provides an illustration: "In water" (jale).
Whatever I say to you should be taken to heart and applied with effort; otherwise, I am not to be questioned by you here in vain.
"Ādeya" means worthy of being taken; "that and that" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Surely there is no difficulty in grasping the meaning of your words, so why do you speak thus? To this he replies:
"O Rāma, the mind is indeed fickle, like a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra; having restrained it within the heart with effort, one must listen to the song of the supreme truth. (MU 2.11.56)

For indeed, because the cessation of the mind necessarily involves effort, and without that effort, it is impossible to take my words to heart; therefore, the sense is that there is certainly effort involved in taking my words to heart.
Now, one might ask: "Having abandoned my own kinsmen, how can I become devoted solely to your words? To this he says:
"Having kept for a long time at a great distance the person who is undiscriminating, ignorant, and fond of the company of the wicked, one must surely honor the virtuous. (MU 2.11.57)
One who lacks knowledge is "ignorant" (*ajñāna*). The sense is that turning away from wicked people and taking delight in the virtuous is the primary means for attaining liberation.
[Objection: "But what will be achieved for me by honoring the virtuous? To this, he says:
"From constant association with the good, discernment arises; enjoyment and liberation are recorded as the two fruits of the tree of discernment. (MU 2.11.58)
This is clear.
"How can such power belong to solitude? To this he replies:
"At the gate of liberation, four gatekeepers are proclaimed: tranquility, discernment, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous."
The sense is that since no one attains liberation without these [factors], whether individually or collectively, discernment (*viveka*) possesses the quality of being a means to liberation.
These four, or else two or three, should be served with effort; they forcibly open the door to the royal palace of liberation.
This is clear.

Or else, one should resort to even a single [virtue] with all one's effort, even at the cost of abandoning one's life; for when this one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
In this one [verse], "one" should be understood as the discerning person (*vivekī*), in accordance with the subsequent verses.
"Now, how will the task be accomplished by this alone? To this he says:
"For one who possesses discernment is the vessel for the scripture, knowledge, austerity, and splendor, just as the sun, in the form of its ornament, is the vessel for its own rays. (MU 2.11.62)
One whose very appearance is an ornament; such is he.
He explains how dullness of wisdom, which is an obstacle to discernment, gives rise to misfortune:
"For in those who lack consciousness, dullness of wisdom, having reached density, attains a state of immobility, like water turning into the hardness of stone through its own coldness. (MU 2.11.63)
When dullness of wisdom reaches a state of density, it becomes fixed; thus it is connected [to the following].
Now, one might ask: "If I am not fit for discernment due to the dullness of my wisdom, what then should be done? To this he replies:
"But you, O Rāghava, have had your inner heart blossomed by kindness, virtuous qualities, and the vision of the meaning of the scriptures; you stand like a lotus at sunrise."
O noble-minded one, you ought to hear and understand this vision of knowledge, just as one whose ear-worm has been extracted is able to perceive the sound of a lute.

The state of being a good person is *saujanya*. Qualities endowed with that are *saujanyaguṇāḥ*. These, along with the insights into the meaning of the scriptures (*śāstrārthadṛṣṭi*), have caused his inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) to blossom—that is, to be free from dullness of intellect. Likewise, he is one whose impurities (*jantumala*) residing in his ears have been extracted and removed. Therefore, he is indeed fit for discernment (*viveka*).
The state of being.
"Now, how is this so? To this he replied:
"O Rāma, that state where no destruction exists is attained through the yoga of dispassion and practice, and by the perfection of equanimity and goodness."
Practice is the study of the true scriptures; that state is the station known as discernment.
He states the means for increasing that discernment which is the ultimate primary goal:

"In the beginning, for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, one should increase wisdom itself through the scriptures, by association with the virtuous, and through well-performed austerity and self-restraint. (MU 2.11.67)
Austerity (*tapas*) is the restraint of the external senses; self-control (*dama*) is that of the internal ones.
One should strive to destroy folly— the foremost watering for the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, the abode of calamities, and the collyrium for the night of delusion.
Delusion is perversion; for by means of ointment, practitioners of mantras manifest night even during the day, and thus it is called "ointment."
"Now, how can my foolishness be destroyed? To this he says:
"Know that this very thing is the supreme destroyer of foolishness: namely, that this scripture is being examined with a somewhat refined intellect. (MU 2.11.69)

“Destruction” means causing destruction. [This occurs] through some refined [speech], merely by knowing certain words and their meanings; it is not through the vast knowledge of the web of grammar which produces agitation. When the heart is possessed by ignorance—endowed with such refinement and leaping within the chest like a serpent of evil desire—the mind undergoes contraction, like a piece of leather placed over a fire.

The "evil desires" are indeed the serpents that are the desire for enjoyments; the meaning is that these evil desires emerge solely from ignorance (*maurkhya*). "Contraction" (*saṃkoca*) refers to the absence of the expansion known as the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cid-vimarśa*).
In the wise person who has become such as it truly is, this vision of reality becomes serene, like the sight of the moon when its entire orb is stainless and free from clouds.
This view of reality (*vastudṛṣṭi*) which I am about to describe is the view of the ultimate truth (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*). It becomes serene; the sense is that it does not find rest even in that [view].
He whose intellect is expansive and endowed with the beautiful skill of investigating what precedes and what follows is called a true man.

The "object of prior and posterior investigation" refers to a matter that has been subjected to examination from beginning to end. She who is adorned with the elegance and skill found therein is *śālinī*.
"You too are such as this," he says with a verse at the end of the canto:
"You shine with a blossoming, white, mind-stealing heart, cool-rayed in its discernment of boons and endowed with virtues, like the sky with the stainless moon."

You shine with a heart that is blossomed—endowed with the expansion called discernment (*viveka*), white—free from the stain of impurity—and captivating, which steals the mind; a heart whose coolness consists precisely in excellent investigation, such a virtuous heart endowed with qualities like loving-kindness (*maitrī*). How so? Just as the sky shines when it is stainless, uncorrupted by impurities such as frost.
The meaning is that it shines with the moon; thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

To steady Śrī Rāma’s mind, the venerable one, his heart fully composed, spoke once more to establish Śrī Rāma’s fitness as an inquirer and his own fitness as a teacher: "O Rāghava, you know how to ask, and you understand what has been said; therefore, I have proceeded to speak with due respect."

O Raghava! You are one whose mind is completely satisfied by being free from the desire for enjoyments; such as you are, you are worthy of honor. You know how to ask questions, and you understand what has been said by me. Therefore, out of respect, I have set about speaking to you;
otherwise, I would not speak—this is the underlying sense.
Having established your mind within the Self—free from passion and ignorance and following pure goodness—remain steadfast to hear this knowledge.
But not upon external objects; having established it, that is, having properly fixed it, within the self.
Indeed, the entire array of qualities belonging to an inquirer exists in you, and the series of qualities of a speaker resides in me, just as the splendor of jewels exists in the ocean.
This is clear.
O sage, through discernment you have attained detachment born of worldly attachment,
just as a moonstone attains moisture when struck by the rays of the moon.
You have taken it up; you have grasped it.
From childhood onwards, you have long practiced with virtuous qualities; you are pure, like a lotus that is naturally clean and possesses long, continuous stalks.
By means of qualities such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, and by means of threads that are *atisaṃtata*—that is, exceedingly uninterrupted.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, listen; I shall tell you the story, for you alone are its worthy recipient. Indeed, without the moon, the pure night-lotus does not blossom."

Whether the discourse on liberation spoken by Brahmā or that which has spontaneously manifested from within, it should be understood that from this point forward, Śrī Vasiṣṭha imparts instruction to Śrī Rāma solely as spoken by Brahmā.
He introduces the discourse on liberation spoken by Brahmā:
"Whatever undertakings there may be, and whatever views there may be—both these and those, upon the realization of the State, indeed come to complete rest."
When the state known as pure consciousness is seen—that is, experienced as one's own self—then, indeed, there is certainty; [therein lies] peace, tranquility.
Now, have these views reached peace for anyone today, or not? To this he says:
If there were no resting of consciousness for one of noble mind, who could endure to contemplate this cycle of existence? MU 2.12.8.

If there were no resting of consciousness— that is, no repose within consciousness itself, within the Self which is the very nature of consciousness— by means of the destruction of the vision of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), then what virtuous person, in this world of transmigration consisting of such suffering, could endure the anxiety that is invariably linked to the failure to attain that repose? Who, indeed, would tolerate such worldly concern?

The meaning is "no one at all. The phrase "like us and others" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The sense is that because he has attained rest, he has no concern whatsoever, which is why he remains here.
"Indeed, where does the thought of one who is capable go? He replied:
"All modes of mentation dissolve through the attainment of the Supreme, like the rocks of the great mountain ranges from contact with the multitude of suns at the end of an eon."

Through the attainment of the Supreme Self, all mental fluctuations—the activities of the mind’s cogitation, that is to say, thoughts—dissolve for one who is fit for liberation. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
“O Rāma, the unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of Yoga. (MU 2.12.10)

Samsara itself is the cholera—meaning a specific disease called cholera—caused by the onset of poison. That is the cholera caused by the onset of the poison of samsara. Indeed, the onset of poison is destroyed by the Garuda mantra.
In response to the inquiry as to how that yoga is attained, he explains in prose:
"And that yoga, consisting of the knowledge of the ultimate reality, is indeed obtained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures in the company of a virtuous person."

“...is indeed obtained,” up to this point is the *ṭīkā*. That yoga, which is the cause for the dissolution of the activity of mental deliberation (*manana*), is indeed obtained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures in the company of a virtuous person; it is not the case that it is not obtained. Of what nature is it? It consists of that knowledge of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is the principle of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-tattva*); it is not of the nature of breath-restraint (*prāṇarodhana*) and so forth.
[Objection: "If nothing at all will be accomplished even through inquiry, then what should be done? To this, he says:
"In this matter, one must consider that when inquiry is certainly performed, there occurs the destruction of all suffering. (MU 2.12.12)
Up to the word "to be considered" (mantavyam), [the meaning] is clear. //MT_2,12.12//
It declares that [this] has borne fruit;

therefore, those with discerning vision should not view [these things] with indifference. By the power of discernment, a person should cast off this entire cage of mental afflictions (*ādhipañjara*), like a snake shedding its mature skin, and find delight with a fever-free and cooled inner mind.
Thus is the entire world perceived by one who possesses right vision.

[The commentary] ends with "by one possessing right vision. [Explanation: Since the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārthatattva*) is obtained only through investigation (*vicāra*), therefore "views of investigation" refers to views known as investigation. They should not be regarded with "contempt," meaning with disregard. Now, one might ask: "What will be accomplished by investigation? To this, he says: "By the power of investigation, by one possessing right vision," that is, by one endowed with right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

By a person who is awakened, the entire world—both external and internal—is viewed as if it were a diversion or a play, because he is free from joy and sorrow occasioned by the presence or absence of those things. By what kind of person? By one for whom this entire experienced world is like a cage of serpents, namely the cage called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), just as a snake sheds its fully ripened skin.
Having renounced [them], he was free from fever, devoid of distress, and for that very reason possessed a cool inner heart.
Now, one might ask: what is the fault in possessing wrong view such that one must resort to right view through investigation? To this he says:

For one who possesses wrong view, this supreme suffering exists; for the disease of *saṃsāra* bites excessively like a serpent, cuts like a sword, pierces like an arrow, and entangles like a rope. [It is] like fire...

It burns like fire; it blinds like night; it renders one helpless like a harsh stone unexpectedly dropped from on high. It carries away wisdom, destroys stability, and casts one into the blind well of delusion. It shatters one with craving.
There is no suffering in saṃsāra that a person does not encounter.

[The commentary] ends with "attains. [The word] *param* means having reached the ultimate limit. Now, one might ask: "By whom was this suffering created for one who possesses right vision? To this, he says: "It is uneven" (*viṣama*). It pierces and strikes. Having realized that a detailed explanation is impossible, he speaks in general terms: "Not that" (*na tat*). One who is in saṃsāra is joined with saṃsāra; therefore, it is precisely by saṃsāra that suffering is produced here for one who lacks right vision.
The sense is that suffering exists.
"Is it not the case that this cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of sense objects, is exactly like this? What does it do to us? To this, he says:
"This [existence] is indeed a chronic cholera of the poison of sense objects. If it is not treated, it leads to the fruit of a multitude of cities of hell;

it produces this and that: where the falling of hundreds of sharp swords is like the striking of blue lotuses, where the burning of fire is like a sprinkling of snow, and where the cutting off of limbs occurs."

The arrangement of sandalwood fans; the friction of whirling winds against the body; the constant falling of a multitude of yak-tail whisks and iron arrows shaken by the flames of incessant fires; the showering of spray from cooling chambers to dispel the summer heat; the severing of the head as a peaceful sleep; the muting of speech as the seal of eloquence; and great accumulation.
"Great accumulation" is the end [of the verse]. The *Ṭīkā* says: "Inevitable" (*durantā*) means impossible to destroy. "Objects" refers to the worldly enjoyments of cyclic existence;

these very things are like the cholera of virulent poison. If that is not treated, then at that time, the result is the mass—that is, the collection—of the cities of hell. Its "consequence" (*anubandha*) is its continuous progression in a stream; that is what follows.

Being such that "it exists in this," she is thus; she produces such and such suffering. In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he says: "Wherein. That is to say, when such suffering exists, or with reference to such suffering, there is a wind that whirls and throbs; within its midst is a crushing, a state of being pulverized, and the rubbing of the limbs.

The meaning is that massage, which brings about softness to the limbs, becomes even more painful when one is in the midst of wind because of being reduced to powder. [This refers to] the falling of a mass of iron arrows (*nārācanikara*) in which there are incessant flames of fire acting like waving chowries (*cāmara*), for the purpose of dispelling the heat— that is, the heat produced by the summer season (*nidāgha*).

For the purpose of distancing [the heat], there are shower-houses; from them, sprays are emitted, and their raining down occurs. *Pāṭavamudrā* refers to the seal (*mudrā*) of proficiency—that is, of skill—where *mudrā* means contraction, meaning emaciation. There is a great accumulation, that is, an increase.
It speaks of the fruit;

therefore, O Rāghava, one must not remain indifferent toward this wheel of saṃsāra, which is so unstable and filled with thousands of such painful strivings. Indeed, this must necessarily be investigated.

This concludes the section to be considered, according to the *Ṭīkā*. Therefore, for that reason, O Rāghava, while this very cycle of existence—which bestows the aforementioned great and harsh sufferings, and is consequently dreadful with its thousands of painful efforts—is being experienced, it is like a flickering machine;
you must not show disregard for it, thinking, "What can this do to me? Furthermore, what should be done? To this, he says: "Necessarily."
Thus, this saṃsāra must necessarily be investigated by the wise; they should bring it within the scope of inquiry as to what "this" is and what "that" is.
"What else is to be done? To this he says:
"And it must be understood in this way: that indeed, through inquiry, there is the attainment of the highest good. (MU 2.12.17)

Thus ends the commentary (*ṭīkā*). A person should understand and resolve it in this way. How so? Just as it is said that through investigation there is the attainment of the highest good, namely the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*).
"Now, does this discrimination belong to anyone, or not? To this he replies:

"Furthermore, O Moon of the Raghu dynasty, if these great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings did not have their bodies enveloped in the armor of knowledge, how could they—being unable to endure suffering—endure the torment of saṃsāra, which consists of suffering and is preceded by the activity of darkness?"
Experiencing this constantly, they remain with minds ever joyful.

The commentary [ends with] "they stand. O moon of the Raghu dynasty! I—and something else—speak; this is the ellipsis. If these great sages, great seers, brahmins, and kings standing before you have their bodies enveloped—that is, covered—by the armor of knowledge, namely the armor called discernment (*viveka*); such are they, endowed with knowledge.

Thus, up to this point: they do not exist. Then, at that time, how is it that these sages and others, though unable to endure suffering, remain with joyful minds—constantly, and not merely occasionally through the attainment of their own desired goals—while experiencing that very suffering consisting of affliction, which is the torment of saṃsāra, preceded by and caused by the activity of darkness (ignorance)? They remain thus.
Therefore, the sense is that there indeed exists a distinction among these.
He states the reason here with a verse interspersed with prose:

"For in this world, just as Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and others remain free from curiosity—that is, devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction—so too do those supreme among men, who have attained the lamp of the Self, remain in the world with awakened intellects.
[End of verse. Commentary: "Hi" means because; "iha" means in this world; "narottamāḥ" means those superior to men, that is, among all human beings.

Among them, those who are the most excellent and supreme; likewise, by whom the Self—that is, the Supreme Self—has been attained and correctly experienced through the power of discernment (*viveka*); such are those of awakened intellects, whose intellects are endowed with discernment, namely the sages and others mentioned previously. They remain in that manner. To the question "In what manner? he says: "free from curiosity" (*vikautukāḥ*).
Thus: "free from curiosity" (vikautukāḥ) means devoid of longing for sense objects; by the word "etc. (ādi), Indra and the others are included.
Thus he speaks of the fruition:

when delusion has been utterly exhausted, when the dense cloud of ignorance has dissolved, when reality has been fully understood, and when the desired Self has been attained; when, having deliberated with the Noble Ones, the nature of both existence and non-existence has dissolved through the intellect and reality has been seen.
This wandering of the world is a source of delight.
[The end of the verse: Commentary. And that being so; *vai* signifies certainty; *āryaiḥ* means with the virtuous ones;

*vicārya* means having investigated both saṃsāra and the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*). When heedfulness regarding delusion—the effect of ignorance—has dissolved, then, when the dense, thick cloud of ignorance itself has melted away, then [the distinction between] the existent and the non-existent...

When the two objects that have become the spheres of the cognitions of "existent" and "non-existent"—having their forms dissolved through the dissolution of those very cognitions of existent and non-existent—are fully known; that is, when the Self, the reality intended as the supreme object of attainment, the reality called the *jīva*, is correctly ascertained as being distinct from the body and so forth; and not merely known, but realized as one's own self through the renunciation of the body and other such things.

When there is correct realization— that is, when the reality of pure consciousness alone has been perceived by the intellect (*dhī*) that is intent upon its own dissolution, and which perceives that reality as the witness to the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth— then this being performed, namely worldly wandering (*aṭana*), which is the activity for the sake of maintaining the body, and sporting (*ramaṇa*), which is play; all these pertain to the world (*jāgata*).
The meaning is that [the self] does not exist, because it lacks the capacity to be affected by joy or sorrow produced by the presence or absence of objects.
And I shall tell you something else, he said:
"Furthermore, O Rāghava, when the essence of consciousness has become serene within the heart, and the Supreme Being dances with full majesty;

when all perceptions of mental constructions have become fully absorbed in the presence [of that Reality]; and when the operations of the internal organ have attained peace—then, through the intellect, one beholds that which is infused with the supreme flavor."
Delighting in reality is wandering through this world.

The end of the verse: *Ṭīkā*—O Rāghava, I say this and something more. "What do you say? To this, he replies: "When [the Supreme] is gracious. When the Supreme—the *cittattva*, the reality known as pure consciousness alone—is gracious, meaning it is oriented toward its own self-manifestation;
for that very reason, when that Supreme *cittattva* is possessed of majesty (*savibhave*), that is, endowed with power (*śaktisahite*), [it abides] in the heart in the form of *sattva*.
When [the Self] is established— meaning when it leaps forth, vibrates within the heart, and comes within the range of reflective awareness— then,
in all perceptions of the manifestation of the universe consisting of living beings and so forth,
which have become fully expanded; that is, when they have become possessed of expansion despite being devoid of expansion through the attainment of the nature of all-pervading pure consciousness.
Then, when the internal instruments— the mental constructs— have been made to enter into tranquility (śama), that is, dissolution into the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) by one's own will,

and as they proceed before him; and thereafter, when reality (tattva)— known as pure consciousness alone— is perceived and experienced as the Self by the intellect (dhī) which is intent on its own dissolution, this wandering through the world becomes a source of delight.
Furthermore, with the same intention as before, he says:
"Moreover, the chariot is the expansive body, the arrangement of horses is the movement of the senses, and the motion is from the wind; I am the unmeasured and infinite Uneven One.
Whether as another or as myself, I, the embodied one, wander through the world"—when the Reality is seen with such stainless intellect, this wandering through the world becomes a source of delight.
This is it. //MU_2,12.22//
Now, the concluding verse of the chapter: [The commentary: The "body" (*deha*) is the gross body. "Expansive" (*sphāra*) means having the nature of vibrating everywhere.

It "becomes a chariot" (*ratha*). The "movement of the senses" (*indriyagati*)—that is, the arrangement of the senses—becomes the "arrangement of horses. This is because, by means of seeing and so forth, it acts as the driver of the body-chariot for the sake of attaining what is desirable and avoiding what is to be rejected, such as forms and other objects. "Vibration" (*parispanda*) refers to the movements of the senses which constitute the arrangement of the horses.

Movement—the capacity to impel the body—arises from the vital air (*vāta*). For it is by means of the vital air that the sense organs, possessing functions such as seeing and so forth, set the body in motion. Or, in another sense, the "embodied one" (*dehī*) is the individual soul (*jīva*) who identifies with the body; he is the "steed" (*arvan*), because ultimately he alone is the mover of the body. He is "ahead of" (*puraḥ*) the body and other such things, being in essence pure consciousness transcending them.

I wander in the world and perform my dwelling. In what state am I? I am one by whom the infinite and uneven perils—in the form of pleasure and pain—are not reckoned, because they have been determined as being my own self and are no longer perceived as sources of suffering. Such is I. For a king, being superior to chariots and the like, remains unaffected by infinite highs and lows; it is with this certainty that I act.

When the reality—whose nature has been described—is perceived by means of an intellect that is stainless, free from defects such as the sense of being bound to the self, and inclined toward liberation, then this wandering through the world becomes a source of delight. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twelfth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Having restated the previously mentioned view, he describes the conduct of those of excellent intelligence by relying upon it:
"Relying on this view, the wise, whose selves are nourished, move about without arrogance, like great beings who have attained their goal. (MU 2.13.1)

Having constantly taken hold of this [state] described in the previous section—that is, having made it the object of their contemplation—those whose selves are nourished; "nourished" meaning their self, known as pure consciousness alone, has reached a state of extreme readiness for manifestation; such persons, being unarrogant and free from pride, appear as if they have risen to power, like those who have obtained a kingdom.
They do not grieve, they do not beg, and they do not desire good or evil; they perform everything, yet they perform nothing at all.

Everything that comes by way of the stream, they perform all of it with the firm resolve, "This must be done. Yet they do not do anything at all, because they lack the conceit of being an agent regarding themselves.

They remain established in their own natural state, they bring others to that same state, and they proceed [in life] free from the dualistic notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, abiding in their own self.

"Composed" (*svastham*) is an adverbial modifier in both cases, meaning "certainly. The meaning is that they are free from the positions of what is to be rejected or accepted, and thus abide in the position of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
They come and yet do not come; they go to the forest and yet do not go. They do not act and yet they act; they speak and yet they do not speak.

In all these cases, action should be understood as occurring through the medium of the body and so forth, which are maintained by one who is liberated while living; non-action, however, occurs through the medium of pure consciousness alone—enough said.

Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever views there may be, and whatever perspectives regarding what is to be abandoned or acquired—these all perish once the state [of the Self] has been realized.
They are exhausted and dissolved; that is to say, they manifest solely as the nature of the supreme state.
The mind that has abandoned all attachment and possesses a sweet disposition attains happiness from every quarter, like the orb of the moon remaining in its place.
Possessing a sweet disposition and endowed with friendliness.
Even the undertaking of emanations, and even the cessation of all curiosity, does not find room within oneself, just as an elixir does not fit within the moon.

It does not fit within, nor can it prevail within, the Self; the sense is that this is because [the Self] consists of absolute bliss (*atyantānandamaya*). The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that even worldly common sense holds that it is illogical for one who is devoid of the impulse to think and devoid of curiosity not to be contained within one's own Self by means of bliss.
*Rasāyana* is the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).
He performs no magical illusions and does not pursue latent tendencies; having cast off the restlessness of a child, he shines forth as the perfect one alone.

Having cast off the fickleness of a child— the restlessness that pursues magical illusions such as traveling through the air, which are accomplished through the power of mantras and the like— he instead brings about their cessation; thus, he shines forth completely, endowed with full contentment.
He states in prose that the contemplation of the reality of the Self alone is the cause for the aforementioned mental dispositions:

"For such dispositions are obtained from the contemplation of the reality of the Self, and not from anything else. Therefore, through inquiry, the Self alone is to be sought, worshipped, and known by a person throughout his life, and nothing else. (MU 2.13.9)

Thus ends the commentary (*ṭīkā*). For (*hi*), because such aforementioned functions (*vṛtti*) and activities (*vyāpāra*)—namely, that very perception (*avalokana*) of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), which is the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasvarūpa*)—are obtained by the person (*puruṣa*) from that alone and not from anything else;
therefore, for as long as one lives, the person must seek the self itself through inquiry. One must investigate: "What is its form?"
Therefore, he is to be worshipped. Here, "worship" (upāsana) should be understood simply as making him the object of continuous, uninterrupted contemplation.

Therefore, he is to be known. He is to be known with certainty as the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), distinct from the gross body and so forth, while the gross body and the rest are not to be known [as the Self]. The word "iti" marks the end of the prose section.
Now, you have established that the observation of the Self must be performed; how, then, will that observation be accomplished? To this, he says in a verse:
"Where there is a single-voiced agreement among one's own experience, the excellent scripture, and the teacher, by means of that continuous practice, the Self is observed. (MU 2.13.10)

One's own innate experience—of that, of the excellent scripture (suśāstra), and of the true teacher (sadguru)—these three, wherein in which practice there may be a single-voiced unity (ekavākyatā), that is to say, a convergence; by means of that continuous and uninterrupted practice, as the instrument, the Self is beheld by the person acting as the agent. (MT 2.13.10)
Even when fallen into dire calamity, one should not become like the foolish—those who disregard the meaning of the scriptures and treat the great men with contempt.
The intention of the word "also" (api) is: how could one who is healthy go [in such a manner]?
In this context, he censures folly:
"Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity exists upon the earth in such a way as to cause distress to men as folly residing within their own bodies does."
This is clear.
Just as this treatise is worthy of being heard by those with some proficiency in Sanskrit, there is no other treatise whatsoever that so effectively dispels ignorance.

"For those with some proficiency in Sanskrit" means for those who know words and their meanings. "Worthy to be heard" means fit for listening. This [work] is called the *Mokṣopāya* (The Means to Liberation). "Dispelling ignorance" means that which destroys ignorance;

this work is worthy of being heard, it brings happiness, and it is beautiful with its narratives and illustrative examples. It is entirely consistent with the meaning and structure of the words of the scriptures.

"By means of narratives" refers to the illustrative examples (dṛṣṭāntas) that will be described; "by those [examples] it is beautiful. That which is the meaning of the statements of the treatise (*śāstra*) is itself the "kinsman"; "not inconsistent with that" means it conforms to the meaning of the treatise.
Those calamities that are difficult to overcome, and those empty, wretched births—all these are produced from folly, just as thorns grow from the khadira tree.
This is clear.
O Rāma, it is better to wander for alms with a bowl in hand through the streets of the outcaste dwellings than to live a life destroyed by folly.
Wandering is roaming about.
Having attained this light consisting of the means to liberation, no person shall ever again fall into blindness, even within the darkness of delusion.
It is light because it illuminates the supreme reality; its very nature is light.
The dark night of craving causes the lotus of man to contract as long as the pure radiance of the sun of discernment has not arisen.
This is clear.
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, one should realize the true nature of the self through the authority of the Guru and the scriptures, together with kinsmen such as myself.

The meaning is: by virtuous persons such as myself. "From the authority of the teacher and the scripture" means from that which is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as the teacher and the scripture. Following the word "having known," the remainder of the sentence is "one should remain [steadfast]."
O Rāghava, conduct yourself here just as Hari, Hara, and others, as well as other Brahman-sages, move about as those liberated while living.
Dwell in the monastery; perform your play by being free from joy and resentment.
In this world, sufferings are infinite, while happiness is like a mere fraction of a moment; therefore, one should not fixate one's vision upon pleasures that are followed by suffering.
In those things connected with suffering and permeated by suffering.
Furthermore, what is to be done? To this he says:
"That state which is infinite and effortless must be achieved with exertion by a discerning person for the sake of attaining the essential goal. (MU 2.13.22)

"Infinite" means devoid of the three kinds of limitations. "Effortless" because it is not to be accomplished through exertion. "For the sake of attaining the essence" means for the sake of accomplishing the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). "It is to be realized" means it should be brought within the range of one's own perception. "By one who knows" means by one endowed with even a slight measure of knowledge, since a fool lacks the qualification for this.
These very persons are the supreme among men, the vessels for the goal of human life, whose minds—free from all feverish distress—rest upon the unsurpassed state.

Because there exists nothing superior to it, it is "unsurpassed" (anuttama), which is to say, "without equal. That which takes as its object such a state (pada) is [described as] "taking such [a state as its object]."
Know those of wicked mind to be like the "blind drum" who are satisfied with mere enjoyments, food, and pleasures such as sovereignty.
"Blind-drum" and "blind-crawlers": the meaning is because they have not seen correctly.
Those who are devoted to the deceitful, the malevolent, those intent on evil deeds, to enemies disguised as friends, and to those who indulge in sensual pleasures; MU_2,13.25.
Those fools, whose intellects are dulled by delusion, go from difficulty to difficulty, from suffering to suffering, from fear to fear, and from one hell to another.
Those whose intellects are slow with delusion and filled with infatuation because they perceive enemies in the guise of friends as being pleasant to the face—such are they.

O Rāma, the two states of pleasure and pain—which are eager to destroy one another, which are never conducive to the highest good, and which are as fragile as a flash of lightning—[should not be clung to].
This is clear.
Know those high-souled men like you, who are dispassionate and perfectly secluded, to be worthy of veneration; they alone partake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And their status as enjoyers of wealth should be understood as occurring only through the natural flow of events, not as something achieved through effort.
Relying upon supreme discernment through the yoga of dispassion and practice, one shall cross over this terrible river of worldly existence and its calamities.
Practice is the practice of the true scriptures; "calamity" means that which has the nature of a calamity.
Indeed, a discerning person who understands this world should not sleep while amidst the illusions of saṃsāra, for they bring about the stupor and delusion of being poisoned.
One must not sleep, nor should one act with contempt.
He who, having encountered this saṃsāra, remains indifferent to it, lies within a high, blazing house made of straw.
Of that which is made of grass, i.e., constructed from grass.
That state, reaching which they do not return and attaining which one no longer grieves, is indeed attainable through wisdom; there is no doubt about this.
It is obtainable through discernment alone, obtainable through intelligence alone; it is not, however, obtainable through external effort.
Now, if that state does not exist, how can it be attained by the intellect? To this he says:
"If it does not exist, what fault would there be for you through its investigation? If it exists, you will have crossed over the ocean of existence."
This is clear.
When a person's inclination here is directed toward investigating the means to liberation, he is then said to be one who partakes in liberation.
This is clear.
In the three worlds, there exists no well-being that is imperishable, free from fear, and devoid of delusion, unless it is the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
Well-being is the state of being healthy; it is the condition of being alone, that is, non-duality, in the absence of the state of a solitary kevalin.
In attaining that—attaining the supreme—affliction is of no use; neither friends, nor wealth, nor kinsmen can provide assistance.
Upon its attainment—that is, upon the attainment of the state of a Kevalin—there is the affliction of the body. //MT_2,13.36//
There is no moving of hands or feet, nor traveling to another land; it is not accomplished through an excess of afflictions, nor does it depend upon sacred fords or shrines.

In this sense, there is no movement of the hands, feet, and so forth; nor is there any travel to another place. This state is not to be accomplished through an excess of afflictions (*kleśa*), nor does it depend upon shrines or sacred sites (*tīrthāyatana*).
That state is attained solely through the conquest of the mind alone—a conquest achieved by human effort as its sole means and whose action has the singular purpose of subduing latent impressions.

That state called *kevalībhāva* (the state of absolute isolation) is attained or reached by the person (*puruṣa*) solely through the conquest of the mind alone. By what kind of conquest of the mind alone? Through that which is human, belonging to the person (*pauruṣa*), and directed toward a single goal (*eka-sādhya*). Furthermore, by what kind? Through that whose activity has the same object as the latent impression (*vāsanā*). *Vāsanā* means mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); that itself is the "single object" (*ekārtha*). Of that...
"By means of action"; the meaning is: "by that which is to be accomplished through mere cultivation."
By abandoning the webs of suffering, that state—which is to be accomplished through solitude alone and is certain through one-pointed inquiry—is attained by a man.

By means of that investigation—that is, by means of discernment (*viveka*) directed toward that object—one attains that which is "one" or absolute; [the word] "whose" refers to that which has certainty as its nature. The meaning is: that which is to be ascertained through investigation. That is the state known as *kevalībhāva* (absolute oneness).
Seated upon a comfortable seat and reflecting upon that [truth] himself, he does not grieve after attaining that state, nor is he born again.
By one who possesses such investigation—that is, by one endowed with the investigation into the state of absolute oneness—that state is the state known as the state of absolute oneness.
The virtuous know that to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that supreme elixir the unsurpassed outflow [of liberation].
This is clear.
Because all states of existence are subject to decay, there is no happiness at all in either heaven or the human realm; it is like water in a mirage.
Of heaven and the human world—that is, of the celestial realm and the terrestrial realm.
Therefore, the conquest of the mind should be contemplated as the means for achieving tranquility and contentment; from that, infinite enjoyment of peace and bliss is attained.
For this reason, a person should contemplate the conquest of the mind. Of what nature is such a person? One for whom tranquility (*śama*) and contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) are the means.
From that conquest of the mind, there arises the enjoyment of infinite tranquility—the wonder, that is to say, the savoring of tranquility; bliss is thus attained.
Whether by one who is living, walking, wandering, or falling, or even by a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human being; MU_2,13.44.
Having attained that supreme bliss arising from the pacification of the mind, one experiences the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment, which has tranquility as its blossoming flower.
Even while engaged in worldly affairs and not accumulating a multitude of tasks, one neither abandons nor hankers after them, like the sun situated in the sky.

Whether living, moving, wandering, or even falling— this is merely an illustration meaning that while performing all activities— whether by a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or a human, that supreme happiness known as *nirvāṇa* is attained by one who remains in the sky [of the mind], being the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment (*viveka*) which blossoms with the flower of expansive tranquility arising from the pacification of the mind.
The meaning is that, like the sun, [the self] is neither abandoned nor desired; rather, equanimity alone is maintained in all circumstances.

By what kind of being—such as a *rakṣas* and so forth? Even by one intent on worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), who does not gather a multitude of tasks (*kāryavṛnda*) because of the certainty that "I am not the doer," and thus does not experience them as his own doing.
The mind, perfectly tranquil, exceedingly clear, rested, and free from delusion, being without effort and devoid of longing, neither desires nor rejects anything.

"Free from effort" means devoid of the activity known as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). "Free from desire" means lacking the certainty that "this is what I desire. The sense is that one acts by means of equanimity alone, as it arises spontaneously in the natural flow.
First, he introduces the determination of the gatekeepers of peace and the other qualities who have been previously mentioned:
"Listen to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order; by devotion to even one of them, one enters the door of liberation. (MU 2.13.48)
Through attachment to one and through cultivation of one.
Therein, he first defines tranquility (*śama*), which was mentioned at the outset:
"The long desert expanse of saṃsāra, filled with the states of suffering and defects, attains coolness for a living being through the cooling water of tranquility. (MU 2.13.49)
That state in which there is the form of suffering and fault is "the state of suffering and fault."
Through tranquility, the highest good is attained, for tranquility is the supreme state; tranquility is auspiciousness, tranquility is peace, and tranquility is the warding off of delusion.
The supreme state is the most excellent abode known as pure consciousness alone.
For a man who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and clear, and whose mind is contented through peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
For it is through hatred alone that one becomes an enemy; since he has no such hatred, the sense is that his enemy attains the state of a friend.
For those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility, supreme purity arises, like that of the oceans of milk.
Supreme purity is the state of being free from the impurity known as latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Those virtuous ones in whose hearts the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotus are indeed like Hari, possessing two lotus-hearts.
The state of being the lotus of the two hearts of Hari should be understood as resulting from the presence of the lotus situated at the navel.
Those whose stainless moon-like faces shine with the beauty of tranquility—they are these venerable moons of their lineage, who have surpassed the [actual] moon in loveliness.
In this case, the very fact of being unstained is the reason for its superiority over the moon.
The splendors existing within the belly of the three worlds do not bring such joy as the manifestations of tranquility, which are the very embodiment of the wealth of universal sovereignty.
This is clear.
Whatever sufferings, whatever cravings difficult to endure, and whatever mental agonies there may be—all that perishes among those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the suns.
This is clear.
For the mind of all beings follows after serenity; it does not do so toward the moon as it does toward a person who is tranquil and has inspired wonder.
Clarity; serenity.
In a virtuous person who possesses tranquility and friendliness toward all living beings, the supreme reality becomes manifest of its own accord.
The supreme reality is the reality of the Supreme Self; it becomes serene by itself, without effort—meaning that it effects a serenity known as the manifestation of its own true nature.
Like a mother, all beings here place their trust in one who possesses tranquility, whether they face hardships or gentleness.
For "viṣamāṇi" means harmful; "mṛdūni" means soft or tender.
