A person does not attain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor through the embrace of Fortune as they do through inner tranquility.
Within the mind.
O Rāghava, comfort this mind, which is enveloped by all manner of mental and physical afflictions and overcome by the threefold bond of craving, with the sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility.
Comfort him; cool him.

Whatever you do and whatever you eat with a mind cooled by tranquility—that is exceedingly sweet and delicious to you, and nothing else; for that which is done with a weary mind does not please, does not delight, and does not produce a sense of wonder.
*Śvadata* means it pleases, it delights, or it produces a sense of wonder. *Tānta* means made weary or dejected. That by which the mind (*mānasa*) is characterized is "that which has a weary mind."
O Rāghava, I believe that even those limbs which have been severed grow back again by means of that peace and bliss which the mind attains when bathed in the nectar-essence of tranquility.
O Raghava, I believe that by means of that bliss which the mind attains when bathed in the nectar-essence of tranquility, even severed limbs grow back again.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Daityas, nor enemies, nor tigers, serpents, and the like, harbor hostility toward one who abides in tranquility.
This is clear.
Arrows do not pierce one whose every limb is well-armored with the nectar-like armor of tranquility, just as they cannot pierce a diamond stone.
They pierce; they strike.
A king does not shine so much when surrounded by his honored harem as he does when adorned with tranquility through a balanced and healthy way of life.
By way of function, that is, by means of activity.
Even upon seeing something dearer than life itself, a person does not attain such satisfaction as that which one attains by beholding a person who is peaceful and of tranquil disposition.
With an even disposition and an even mind.
He who conducts himself well with a conduct that is disciplined and tranquil, and which is welcomed by the world, truly lives here; no one else does.
It proceeds, that is, it persists; the other is unpeaceful.
Whatever virtuous deed one who is undisturbed in mind and tranquil performs, all these beings rejoice in it.
They rejoice and offer praise.
He determines the nature of tranquility by means of defining the nature of peace:
"Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, and smelled what is auspicious and inauspicious, he who neither rejoices nor desponds is said to be tranquil. (MU 2.13.70)
The sense is that equanimity itself is peace.
He who is equanimous toward all things, neither desiring nor rejecting, having conquered the senses through effort—he is called "peaceful."
This is clear.
He whose mind is as clear as the orb of the moon and remains undisturbed even in the face of death, festivities, or battle, is said to be "peaceful."
This is clear.
Even when standing, he is as if not standing; he neither rejoices nor is he provoked to anger. He whose mind is as if in deep sleep and who is established in his own nature is said to be "peaceful."
With a mind in deep sleep, he is devoid of the pursuit of joy or resentment.
He whose joyful gaze, lovely with the flow of nectar, extends toward every person, is called "peaceful."
This is clear.
He whose actions are perceived with a clear and pure intellect, such that they are exactly the same internally as they are externally, is said to be "peaceful."
The meaning is that it is due to the absence of deceit.
Even in calamities that end in despair, even when the world is being consumed at the end of an aeon, he whose mind does not consider this world to be trivial is said to be peaceful.
This world is hollow, devoted to hollow means.
He who has attained inner coolness, who does not sink into worldly phenomena, and who engages in worldly affairs without delusion—he is said to be at peace.
He does not sink because he is unattached despite the intensity of passion; he engages in worldly activity, performing his duties. He is not deluded, yet he is not devoid of worldly activity.
For in one who is devoid of worldly activity, the absence of sinking is caused precisely by the lack of activity itself, not by peace.
He whose mind, like space, is always free from blemish as he engages in his own worldly affairs, is said to be "peaceful."
"Sva" means one's own; it refers to such a person who possesses worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).
Among ascetics, the learned, sacrificial priests, and kings—among those who are powerful and rich in virtues—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines.
This is clear.
For the great ones who possess virtue and whose minds are absorbed in tranquility, bliss arises from the heart like moonlight from the moon.
This is clear.
The glorious tranquility of the wise shines forth as the boundary of all multitudes of virtues, the singular ornament of manliness, and the place of fearlessness in times of distress.
This is clear.
He concludes the exposition on tranquility with this verse at the end of the canto:

"Having relied upon that supreme state—tranquility, which is immortal, unassailable, and cherished by the noble—you have proceeded to the highest goal, O high-souled descendant of Raghu; therefore, maintain that very same sequence for the sake of your own perfection."

O son of Raghu! Just as those men of great majesty—who attained immortality that is of the nature of nectar, which is indestructible, imperishable, and cherished by the noble—reached the supreme state, the exalted abode whose nature is supreme consciousness, by relying upon tranquility (*śama*) of the previously described character; so do you likewise maintain that same course for the sake of perfection. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 2,13 //
Oṃ. With a mind made pure by the stainless understanding of the scriptures and supremely purified, one who knows the cause should constantly engage in inquiry into the self. MU 2.14.1.
What is the use of one who knows the cause—that is, a person who knows by what [means] one succeeds? One must constantly perform an investigation of the self through the intellect.
[Objection: "But what will be accomplished by inquiry? To this he replies:
"Having attained sharpness through inquiry, the intellect perceives the supreme state; for inquiry is indeed the great medicine for the disease of long-lasting saṃsāra. (MU 2.14.2)
The supreme state, the great abode known as pure consciousness alone.
The forest of calamities, whose form is made to sprout by endless desires, does not grow again once it has been cut down by the saw of discernment.
That whose form was fully blossomed—that is, nourished—by those infinite desires and activities.
O one of great wisdom, in delusions, in the loss of kinsmen, in calamities, and in errors—in all these indeed, discernment is the refuge of the virtuous.
The goal is the refuge.
Without investigation, there is no means to pacify the afflictions; by means of investigation, the minds of the virtuous abandon the unwholesome and attain the wholesome.
This is clear.
Strength, intelligence, vigor, comprehension, and the fruit of action—all these bear fruit for the wise man through discernment alone.
Practice is knowledge; however, the meaning is that these [actions], when performed without discrimination, produce only harm.
Relying on extensive investigation, which is a great lamp for what is appropriate and inappropriate and which accomplishes one's desires, one shall cross the ocean of saṃsāra.

The meaning is that this is a great lamp for what is appropriate and inappropriate, illuminating that "this is appropriate" and "this, however, is inappropriate. It is *sphāram*, which means extensive.
The noble lion of inquiry, being a pure self, tears asunder the great elephant of delusion whose lotus-heart has been lacerated.
It tears asunder; it destroys.
That even the deluded, by the power of time, have reached the supreme state in this world is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry.
For even the deluded, in due time, attain the supreme state known as pure consciousness alone; this is its unfolding, its play, which is unsurpassed and beyond all comparison.
Kingdoms, abundant prosperity, expansive enjoyment, and eternal liberation—these, O Rāghava, are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry.
This is clear.
Those minds of the great in this world which delight in solitude do not sink in adversity, just as gourds do not sink in water.
Because they possess this discernment (*viveka*), they are called *vivekavilāsinyaḥ* (those who delight in discernment).
Those who conduct themselves with an intellect that captivates through the arising of discernment indeed become the recipients of most exalted fruits.
By means of that which captivates through the arising of discernment, and which is enchanting to the mind.
The successions of suffering are the blossoms of the *karañja* trees of non-investigation, which reside in the forest of the fool’s heart and obstruct the expansion of hope.

Hope is the hope for liberation; those who obstruct its expansion are such as they—those who block the spreading of the quarters. Of these *karañja* trees, which are thorny shrubs, there are painful arrangements and painful structures.
O Rāghava, may your sleep—which is as dark as soot-powder, which bears the fragrance of wine, and which consists of a lack of discernment—come to an end.

With the soot-powder consecrated by mantra; "soot-powder" means dark and thick, or like soot-powder, it is dark due to extreme turbidity. Wine bears joy, thus it is such [a wine]. Even by the fragrance of wine, sleep becomes dense. The sense is:
"bring that very [sleep], which consists of non-discernment and has non-discernment as its nature, to destruction."
Even during great calamities or long-lasting hardships, a person devoted to right reflection does not sink into delusions, just as a mass of light does not sink into darkness.
Regarding such matters as "What shall I do amidst delusions? and so forth?
He in whose pure mental lake the multitude of lotuses that are reflection has surely blossomed shines like the Himalaya.
In the lake of the mind, in the lake known as the heart, and in the lake called Mānasa.
For one whose intellect has become dull due to a lack of discernment, a thunderbolt falls from the moon as fruitlessly as a phantom rises before a child.

"Devoid of investigation" means lacking discernment. "Dullness" is stupidity. "From the moon" means from cyclic existence, which is like the moon because it is of the nature of a reflection of the sun of consciousness. "The thunderbolt" refers to the vajra consisting of joy and resentment produced by the presence or absence of phenomena; and it is a marvel that a thunderbolt should arise from the moon.
O Rāma, that lowest of men who lacks discernment must be abandoned from afar; he is a pit of misery, a termite mound, and a spring for the withered creepers of calamity.
What is the lowest of men? Suffering. What is for eunuchs? An anthill—for indeed, thorny shrubs grow upon an anthill. Again, what is it? Misfortune itself is a fresh creeper.
Its spring is whatever ill-conceived undertakings, wicked conducts, and evil anxieties there may be; without investigation, these appear like vampires in the darkness.
"Bad undertakings" refers to contemptible actions that have been commenced.
O scion of the Raghus, keep far away from one who lacks discernment, who is like a solitary, withered tree, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds.

Standing in a solitary place devoid of people is like an aged tree; it is similar to that [tree] in its nature. In noble deeds such as the restraint of the mind and so forth, as well as in acts of benefiting others through the giving of fruit, the mind of a living being is indeed secluded, freed from the helplessness of desire, and attains supreme bliss within itself, like the full moon.

"Secluded" means endowed with solitude. "Free from the helplessness of desire" is stated by way of a qualification as the reason; for it is precisely the helplessness of desire that obstructs tranquility.
Discrimination, once arisen, thoroughly cools the entire body and adorns it exceedingly, like a fresh moonlight adorning the world.
It is fresh, belonging to the autumn season.
For a living being, the investigation of the intellect—which is the white chowrie of the banner of ultimate truth—shines forth like the moon in the night.

Of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is called the reality of pure consciousness alone; of the intellect (*dhī*), which has taken the form of a banner (*patākā*) as a sign by virtue of its common characteristic of being a pointer; [it is] like a white chowrie (*dhavalacāmara*), in that it bestows beauty.
States that are delightful when investigated shine forth, illuminating the ten directions like the sun, having destroyed the disease of the fear of repeated existence.

Existents are entities such as humans and the like. Of what nature are these existents? They are those by whom many fears of worldly existence have been shattered, which are themselves like diseases. Even the sun, though it illuminates the ten directions, is a life-taker imagined through the delusion of one's own mind for a child; yet at night in the darkness, that very specter (vetāla) dissolves through inquiry.
This is clear.
All worldly phenomena are beautiful only so long as they are not investigated; their true existence is non-existent, for they fall apart under scrutiny.
All worldly phenomena—all things in the world—are beautiful when not subjected to analysis—that is, when devoid of investigation.
Of what nature are they? They are such that their true existence is non-existent. For this very reason, they are fragile under analysis, because they cannot withstand critical examination.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra—which, imagined by a person’s own deluded mind, bestows no small amount of suffering—dissolves through inquiry.
This is clear.
Know this state of absolute oneness to be equally pure, free from affliction, infinite, and the refuge of no-mind; it is the fruit of the supreme tree of discernment.
"Equally" (*samaṃ*) means "equally clear" (*samasvacchaṃ*). "Unobstructed" (*nirābādhaṃ*) means it cannot be contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Of the infinite and undelimited reality of one's own self (*svātmatattva*), that which is "reflection" (*manana*)—that is, awareness (*parāmarśa*)—is its "basis" (*āśraya*); this is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to mean its "accomplisher" (*sādhaka*).
By him, through his unwavering stability and the splendor of his vast, manifest majesty, he arises with dispassion, like the coolness produced by the risen moon.

By him who possesses such splendor—whose expansive manifestation is noble and whose wide extension is preeminent; by him, moreover, by that risen moon, which is characterized by freedom from desire (niṣkāmatā) and the absence of longing.
"Now, what will be accomplished by freedom from desire? To this he replies:

"By that [freedom from desire], which is a great medicine for the fever of anxiety, well-established in the mind and bestowing the state of excellence, one neither longs for nor abandons. (MU 2.14.30)
By that state of desirelessness, he neither longs for nor rejects; the meaning is that he maintains equanimity toward everything.
Furthermore, what does it do? To this he says:
That mind, having the true as its object, has become expansive and luminous; it neither sets nor rises, like the sky with its exceedingly vast interior. (MU 2.14.31)

That state of desirelessness is its constant object and support; thus, it is "that which has that as its constant object. Likewise, it is expansive, having the nature of radiating; the meaning is that it has come into manifestation and become endowed with discernment.
It neither abandons nor grasps, it neither exerts itself nor becomes tranquil; merely observing like a witness, it remains within the self while beholding the world.
He does not despair, nor is he agitated.
It is neither extinguished, nor does it abide within or without; it does not take up inaction, nor does it sink into actions.
The meaning is that he conducts himself with equanimity alone in all circumstances.
He remains equanimous toward what has passed and follows what has arrived; neither agitated nor excessively unagitated, he shines like a full ocean.
It follows along; it proceeds without further connection; "ati" means exceedingly.
With such a mind, the great-souled ones of noble intent—yogis who are liberated while living—indeed wander about in this world.
This is clear.
Having dwelt for a very long time, as long as they desire, those wise ones finally abandon the body and attain the pervasive state of absolute oneness.
"Kevalatām" means the state of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*). By the phrase "as long as desired," it is indicated that everything performed by the Blessed One constitutes their very desire.
Even in times of adversity, the wise person should diligently reflect with a remedial mindset: "Who am I, and whose is this saṃsāra? MU 2.14.37.

What need is there to say more? This is the intended meaning of the word "api" (even). It is not merely by reflection alone, but with a remedy—that is, accompanied by a remedial measure. And here, the remedy should be understood as the very renunciation of enjoyment.
O Raghava, the king knows the doubt regarding the difficulty of the task—whether it will be fruitless or fruitful—only through deliberation, and not otherwise.
The sense is that even externally, the sovereignty belongs to investigation alone.
The established tenets of the Vedas and Vedānta, which are the cause of stability, are determined through inquiry, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp.

The "establishments" (sthitayaḥ) consist of the Vedas and the Vedāntas; they are the boundaries (maryādāḥ), that is, the established limits of the Vedas and Vedāntas. They are the causes of establishment, serving as the cause for the boundaries of saṃsāra.
Discernment, like an eye of exquisite vision, does not fail even in darkness; it is not dimmed even by great brilliance, and it perceives even that which is obstructed.

For when the eye is directed toward a brilliance that is not blinding, it becomes "jihmita"—that is, it undergoes a turning away due to the impact [of the light]; the meaning here is that such a thing does not occur in this case.
For one who is blind to discernment is born-blind, a fool to be pitied by all; but he whose soul is discernment and who possesses the divine eye triumphs over all things.
The meaning is that he is to be pitied by everyone; "one whose self is discernment" (*vivekātmā*) means one who possesses discernment. "He triumphs" means he exists with supreme excellence.
Consisting of the Supreme Self, to be protected, and the sole means to great bliss—the wondrous power of discernment must not be abandoned for even a single moment.
She is to be protected and guarded.
A man who is charming in his discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a fully ripened mango fruit is delightful.
This is clear.
Men whose minds delight in reflection, having known the upward path, do not again and again tumble into the many abysses of suffering.
Known means attained; when consciousness alone has transcended upward, that is the goal to which one goes.
Neither does a sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes wail as much as the ignorant man whose soul is ruined by a lack of discernment.

In the phrase "worn out by hundreds of misfortunes," the word *ca* (and) is to be supplied. One who is "destroyed" or "forgotten" through lack of inquiry—that is, through lack of discernment—is one whose *ātman*, or ultimate true nature, has been lost. Such is the person described.
Better to be a worm in the mud, better to be a thorn in a pit, better to be hidden in a blind cave, than for a man to lack discernment.
This is clear.
One should abandon that which is the natural abode of all misfortunes, despised by all the virtuous, the ultimate limit of all wretchedness, and devoid of discernment.
All those misfortunes—of them, this [body] is the innate, one's own abode; the meaning is that it is the locus of all misfortunes.
A great-souled person must always be engaged in inquiry; for indeed, inquiry is the support for those falling into the dark well of worldly existence.
For "hi" has the sense of "because"; "avalambana" means a support or basis.
By firmly supporting oneself with one's own self and investigating through inquiry, one may cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra.
By means of the self, that is, by means of the mind; having firmly grasped the self, the supreme self, through meditative cultivation.
He describes the nature of investigation (vicāra):
"Who am I? How has this defect called saṃsāra come upon me? By what reasoning?"—such reflection is called investigation. (MU 2.14.50)
By means of logic and reasoning; thorough reflection is continuous cultivation.
The heart of the foolish and unreflecting person has long been made like a stone—blind, deaf, and noisy with delusion, serving only for suffering.

"Exceedingly blind" means utterly blind; such is that which is "mouthy with delusion," meaning it is possessed of confusion through dullness. It should be understood as leading to suffering for both oneself and others.
For in this world, O Rāghava, for those who hold views of grasping at existence and non-existence or of rejecting them, no reality whatsoever is properly known except through inquiry.
*Graha* means grasping; *utsarga* means relinquishing.
From inquiry, reality is known; from reality, rest in the Self arises; thence comes tranquility of mind and the complete destruction of all suffering.

The reality is that which is called pure consciousness, the supreme reality. Within the self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, he describes the essential nature of tranquility with the words "all," etc.; for the cessation of all suffering is itself the very form of tranquility.
He concludes the exposition of inquiry with this verse at the end of the chapter:
"The fruitfulness of actions indeed bears fruit on earth for one who attains eminence;
may that which has been clearly investigated through the vision of inquiry shine forth even for you, who are possessed of tranquility. (MU 2.14.54)

Indeed, it is certain that on this earth the fruitfulness of actions bears fruit through the very eye of clear discernment—that is, by means of that discernment which is itself manifest. This is because discernment (*viveka*), especially when arising from the highest source, possesses the power to reveal everything.
Therefore, may this [work], having been thus scrutinized, be pleasing even to you, who possess tranquility. May there be auspiciousness! (MT 2.14.54)
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ. Having thus determined the nature of inquiry, [the Lord] describes the nature of the third [virtue], contentment: "Contentment is the highest good; contentment is said to be happiness. O slayer of enemies, one who is contented attains supreme rest. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.15.1)
A contented person is one who is endowed with contentment.
For the virtuous who find happiness in the sovereignty of contentment and whose minds have long been at rest, even a universal empire is like a mere fragment of withered grass.
This is clear.
O Rāma, an intellect characterized by contentment regarding the conditions of worldly existence is never distressed, remaining unperturbed even amidst adversities.
He is not distressed nor tormented, for he is contented.
For those who have attained supreme satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, even incomparable worldly splendor acts like a potent poison.
*Prativiṣāyate* means it acts like *prativiṣā*; *prativiṣā* is a specific kind of bitter substance.
These waves of nectar-like flavor do not satisfy one as much as contentment, which possesses a sweet taste and destroys all defects.
This is clear.
By way of describing the nature of contentment, he explains the essence of contentment itself:

"Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained, having reached equanimity toward what has been obtained, and being inwardly free from distress regarding the unseen—that person is called 'content' in this world. (MU 2.15.6)
When it has arrived, having come in its natural flow.
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the Self, so long do calamities arise from the forest of the mind like creeping vines.
By oneself, that is, by one's own [nature], and not by means of enjoyment and so forth.
The mind, cooled by contentment, attains full blossoming through the vision of pure gnosis, just as a lotus does under the rays of the sun.
The sense is that only one who is content has the qualification for knowledge.
In a mind rendered helpless by the powerlessness of desire and devoid of contentment, knowledge does not reflect, just as it does not appear in a mirror clouded by a withered face.
It reflects and adheres.
The lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the dense night of ignorance, for that sun of contentment has risen within him forever.
That lotus of a man does not undergo contraction through the thick night of ignorance; what is it? It is that for which this sun of contentment is perpetually risen.
Even though he possesses nothing, that person enjoys the happiness of sovereignty, for his mind is contented and liberated from mental and physical afflictions.
This is clear.
He who does not desire what has not been attained, and who enjoys what has been attained in due order—he, O gentle one, being of good conduct, is called "contented."
This is clear.
In the mouth of the great man who is fully satisfied with contentment and whose mind is complete—like the pure ocean of milk—the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendent.
This is clear.
Fully relying upon perfection within one's very own self by means of the self itself, one should abandon craving everywhere through human effort.
Fullness and contentment; by the self alone, and not by enjoyments—this is the meaning.
For one who is filled with the nectar of contentment, a natural coolness arises within the mind; for one who is not empty [of this], stability becomes eternal, like that of the moon.
Within oneself means in one's own mind; of the non-empty means of the full.
With minds nourished by contentment, those of great prosperity attend upon him like servants, having entered into a state of servitude.
Just as servants who have entered into the state of servitude attend upon a king, so too do those of great supernatural power attend upon one whose mind is nourished by contentment.
When the person remains established within the self by the self alone, in a state of clarity and contentment, all mental anxieties are quickly pacified, like dust in the rainy season.
In that which is clear and free from the impurities of passion and so forth.
A person shines with a pure mode of conduct that is eternally cool and free from blemish, like the full moon.
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of certainty; [she was] with one free from blemish, that is, devoid of the stain known as discontent.
He concludes the exposition on contentment with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"O descendant of Raghu, even the sky-dwelling great sages bow down to that stainless man who, being a king among men, is adorned here by his equanimity and his mind endowed with virtues. (MU 2.15.19)
This is clear. May there be auspiciousness. MT_2,15.19.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. // 2.15 //

Oṃ. Having thus determined the nature of contentment, [the author] now specifically describes the fourth [means], association with the virtuous (satsaṅga), for the crossing over of worldly existence by men: "In every way, O Great-Minded One, the company of the virtuous here in this world is beneficial to all. (MU 2.16.1)
This is clear.
Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
Of the glory of the fruit—that is, of the splendor of the fruit known as liberation.

An empty place becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival; and misfortune appears like prosperity in the assembly of wise men. (MU 2.16.3) "Empty" (*śūnya*) means a desolate region; "crowdedness" (*ākīrṇatām*) means a place filled with people. Frost is the adversity of the lotus-pond, and the mist is the wind of delusion. Victorious alone in this world is the meeting of the virtuous with the virtuous. (MU 2.16.4)
Excellent, it is right.
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the destroyer of the tree of ignorance, and the complete dispeller of mental anxieties.
"Samutsāraṇa" means destruction.
From association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment arises—truly as enchanting and radiant as a cluster of blossoms from an *aśoka* tree.
This is clear.
The riches of association with the virtuous bestow that which is free from disease, free from affliction, eternally abundant, and unsurpassed: namely, nirvāṇa.
This is clear.
Even by men who have fallen into a most miserable state and have become helpless, association with the virtuous must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree.
This is clear.
In this world, associations with the virtuous are the auspicious lamps for the path of the righteous; they are the rays of the sun of knowledge that dispel the darkness within the heart.
This is clear.
For one who has bathed in the cool, white Ganges of association with the virtuous, what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
This is clear.
O sinless one, if there exist holy men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots have been unraveled, what is the use of asceticism or visiting sacred fords?
With their knots loosened, the knots known as desire have been destroyed.
Indeed, those whose minds are at rest are worthy of worship through supreme effort; for the virtuous must be gazed upon with great care, just as a poor man gazes upon jewels.
This is clear.
The intellect of the wise, graced by the beauty of association with the virtuous, shines forever like a lotus amidst a host of celestial nymphs.
Kamalā is Lakṣmī.
By that fortunate one who did not abandon association with the virtuous, the state of being a flower-cluster at the tip of the foot of stainless grace was thus woven.

By that man—by one who is auspicious and of a divine nature—the state known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is stainless, playful, and endowed with pure radiance, has been made its crest-ornament, its crowning glory. The sense is this: association with the virtuous (*sādhusaṃgati*) has not been abandoned; indeed, association with the virtuous must be cultivated, for it shines resplendent within the state called pure consciousness.

Those who have severed the knots, who possess that knowledge, who are virtuous, and who are honored by all—these should be served by every means, for they are indeed the means for crossing the ocean of existence.
This is clear.
These very people have become the dried-up fuel for the fires of hell—those who, with indifference, beheld the virtuous as if they were the waters that extinguish the fires of hell.
This is clear.
The turbulent delusion that poverty, death, and suffering are [the ultimate] miseries is completely pacified by the medicine of association with the virtuous.
This is clear.
Contentment, association with the virtuous, reflection, and tranquility— these alone are the means that men conceive for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
This is clear.
Contentment is the supreme gain; association with the virtuous is the supreme goal; inquiry is the supreme knowledge; and tranquility is indeed the supreme happiness.
The intended meaning of the phrase "the supreme state" (*parapada*) is that beyond this, there is no further gain or attainment.
These four are the stainless means for shattering cyclic existence; those who have practiced them have crossed over the ocean of existence, which has delusion as its waters.
From the sword of delusion, which is possessed of the water known as delusion.
O best among the wise, when even one of these has been cultivated and pure emergence occurs, all four are indeed said to have been cultivated.
This is clear.
Even a single one among all these is like the source of birth for them all; therefore, for the sake of achieving everything, one should diligently rely upon a single one.
The place of birth is the locus of origination.
But contentment with the company of the virtuous and discernment proceed without being sought after, like currents in an ocean that is clear through tranquility.
Vehicles are the movement of water; this is beyond doubt and free from deliberation.

In a living being who frequents the company of the virtuous, discernment, contentment, and tranquility arise, just as the powers of the wish-fulfilling tree manifest in one who has taken refuge under it.
This is clear.
In a person endowed with contentment, discernment, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous proceed, just as beauty and other qualities appear in the full moon.
This is clear.

Association with the virtuous, contentment, and tranquility prevail in one who possesses right-mindedness and reflection, just as the glories of victory attend a preeminent minister in matters of statecraft.
Among the ministers who know the secret counsels, he is the most excellent and supreme.
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having conquered the mind—which is one among these [six] and is eternal—by means of human effort, one should diligently cultivate virtue."
Therefore, from among these four, one should bring forth—that is, acquire—one quality in the form of contentment or another such virtue.
Relying on supreme human effort and having conquered the elephant of the mind, as long as even a single virtue is not attained, there is no higher state.
This is clear.
O Rāma, with manly effort, grinding tooth against tooth, [strive] until your mind is firmly resolved upon the acquisition of virtue.
Whether you are a god, a yakṣa, a human, or even a tree, O mighty-armed one, there is no means whatsoever for you here [to escape] until then.
In the acquisition of virtues, that is, in the acquisition of contentment and so forth.
When even a single quality has borne fruit and attained strength, all the defects of the undiscerning mind quickly perish.
The defects are attachment and so forth.
When virtue increases, virtues that bring about the destruction of faults also increase; when vice increases, vices that destroy virtues also increase.
This is clear.
For in this great forest of the mind, the swift river of latent impressions (vāsanā), with its vast banks of the auspicious and inauspicious, flows constantly among living beings.
This is clear.
For she flows along whichever bank she is cast upon by one's own effort; therefore, act however you wish.
For "hi" indicates certainty; that is the river of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O one of excellent resolve, gradually lead the great river of your own nature along the auspicious banks within the forest of the mind by the speed of human effort; for in this way, you will not be carried away even slightly by it."

By the speed of human effort, by the force of manly exertion—[thinking], "Why indeed should I not bring this river of my own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) to its bank?"—in response to this expectation, he says: "For here... For (*hi*) because of that, by following the auspicious bank of that great river of one's own nature, you are not carried away helplessly, nor led here and there by that great river of your own being, as it has reached the bank.
And nothing at all is carried away by the river. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus he speaks of the fruition:
"O Rāghava, one who has thus attained solitude is fit to hear the words of knowledge, just as a king is fit to hear the speech on statesmanship."

O Raghava, this being so, that person who possesses discernment becomes worthy of hearing words of wisdom, just like your majesty. Like whom? Like a king; just as a king is worthy of hearing the speech of policy—that is, the sayings of political ethics—so it is here.
This is the meaning.
Pure, possessing a great disposition for pure consciousness, and abandoned by attachment to the dull, he is fit [for liberation], just as the autumnal sky is for the moon.

"Pure" (*avadāta*) means free from the impurities of passion and the like through the practice of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth; it is also "stainless" (*nirmala*). Because the pure object is mere consciousness (*cinmātra*), it is "white" (*śuddha*). It is "abandoned by association with the dull" (*jaḍasaṅgojjhita*), meaning it is relinquished by association with the deluded; the sense is that it does not perform [such] action. Furthermore, by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it means it is abandoned by association with the "dull," namely the clouds.
Supported by this unimpaired splendor of virtue, listen to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind.
This is clear.
This effort to hear [this teaching] belongs to that person for whom the wish-fulfilling tree of merit stands bowed under the weight of its fruit, leading to the liberation of living beings.
This is that treatise.
Only a person of noble character becomes a vessel for words that are purifying, sublime, and bestowing the singular realization of the Supreme—for their own prosperity; not one who is base.
The fortunate one possesses a divine nature.
This compendium, equal in essence to the *Sāra*, is titled *Mokṣopāya*; consisting of thirty-two thousand verses, it bestows liberation upon those who know it.
The *saṃhitā* is the science; it is "equal to the essence," meaning identical to the essential truth; it has been "known," that is, thoroughly investigated.
"Now, what will be accomplished by this? To this he replies:
"Just as when a lamp is lit for one who is awake, light arises even though he does not desire it, so too shall there be nirvāṇa through this."

Just as when a lamp is lit, light arises for one who is half-asleep and half-awake— even if they do not desire it and have no longing for light— so too, by means of this *saṃhitā*, there shall be Nirvāṇa, which is the absolute dissolution into Brahman.

Whether known by oneself or heard from another, it bestows happiness solely through the pacification of delusion; when described as the words of a reliable authority, it immediately [bestows it] like a wave of nectar.
"Described by the words of a trustworthy person" is the reason for [the term] "heard," expressed by way of its qualification.
Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope perishes through inspection, so too does the suffering of saṃsāra come to rest through this contemplation.
The examination and investigation of this compendium constitute "this examination"; therefore [it is so called].
In this work, there are six chapters consisting of sentences with logically consistent meanings, each composed separately, and containing well-spoken essences of illustrative examples.

I have composed and established six treatises (*prakaraṇa*) in this [work]. Of what nature are they? They consist of sentences endowed with meaning (*arthavākya*). Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are those in which the well-spoken words (*sūkta*) are excellent and essential, being joined with logical reasoning (*yukti*) and accompanied by illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
He specifically points out the six chapters:
the chapter named "Detachment" is proclaimed as the first; by means of it, detachment increases like a tree in a desert through irrigation.
"Now, what is accomplished by that? To this he says: "Detachment. (MT 2.17.11)
In response to the inquiry as to what its extent is, he says:
"It consists of one thousand five hundred verses; when this is reflected upon in the heart, pure luminosity arises, like [clarity] in a gem that has been polished. (MU 2.17.12)

The word "of the work" (*granthasya*) is used in the singular to denote the class (*jāti*). That section on detachment (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*) consists of one thousand five hundred verses of the work. What is it? When that heart is contemplated, a manifest, clear purity—freedom from the stains of passion and so forth—arises. Like what? Like a gem when it has been polished and cleansed; just as [purity arises] when it has been thoroughly rubbed clean.
Purity arises in the jewel; such is the meaning. // MT_2,17.12 //
Thereafter, the section titled "The Conduct of One Seeking Liberation" was composed; it consists of approximately one thousand verses and is beautiful with its string of well-spoken words.
That which is a composition in the form of well-spoken verses (*sūkti*) is a sentence; by that, it is beautiful—meaning it is endowed with that.
Now, what is it that is being described there? To this he says:
"For the nature of men who seek liberation is described therein; thus it is understood that one of such a nature is fit for liberation. (MU 2.17.14)
"Now, what will be accomplished by this description? To this, he says: "It has such an intrinsic nature."
Then follows the section on Origination, consisting of parables and narratives, comprising five thousand verses, which establishes the nature of consciousness.
The meaning is that "the demonstration of consciousness" (vijñānapratipādana) is that which demonstrates consciousness (vijñānapratipādaka).
The glory of the world, consisting of the seer and the seen, and taking the form of "I" and "you," is described as being where it is neither arisen nor yet arisen.
This is clear.
Upon hearing which, this entire world—including ourselves, you, its vast extent, and the space of the worlds along with its mountains—is understood within the interior of the ear.
It is free from the grasping of a solid mass, without foundations and without mountains, devoid of the primary elements such as earth, like a city created by mere imagination.
In whatever context of origination [is discussed], that which is associated with "I" and "you"—namely, the notion of "I-ness"—is what is perceived.

Regarding the phrase "it is perceived," the word "hearer" (*śrotr*) should be supplied as the agent. In response to the question "What kind of thing is perceived?", he says: "the grasping of a mass," and so forth.
For in conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*), a city appears exactly in this way; thus, it is employed as an illustration.

Furthermore, of what nature is that which is perceived? To this he says: "It is like an object perceived in a dream, spread out like a kingdom of the mind, resembling a city of the Gandharvas—an apprehension devoid of any real object. (MU 2.17.19)

The meaning is that it resembles the appearance of entities perceived in a dream, being similar to objects seen in a dream. Gandharvas, for the sake of their own dwellings, imagine a city in the sky through conceptualization; that is precisely what a "gandharva-city" is. It is devoid of objective reality, lacking such real entities as jars and so forth, yet it is characterized by perception—that is, cognition—within it.
It appears like the delusion of two moons, spread out like the water of a mirage, resembling mountains seen from a moving boat, and is utterly devoid of the attainment of truth.
This is clear.

It resembles a demon that causes the mind to wander, yet it is seedless and radiant; it appears like the inspired eloquence regarding the meaning of the teachings, and is comparable to a string of pearls suspended in the sky.

"Seedless" (*nirbījam*) means devoid of a cause. Regarding the "subject matter" (*artha*) of the discourse—that is, the entity (*padārtha*) to be described—the "inspiration" (*pratibhāna*) is its vivid manifestation as if standing before one. That [speech] has that [manifestation] as its radiance (*ābhā*). For in discourse, the entity to be described appears as if situated right in front. "The sky" (*vyoma*): for indeed, due to an optical illusion, a string of pearls is seen in the sky.

Just as the state of being a bracelet [is unreal] in gold, just as the state of being a wave [is unreal] in water, and just as blueness [is unreal] in the sky, so too has that which is non-existent arisen.
Just as bracelets and the like, though non-existent, arise within gold, so too the world, though non-existent, is perceived as having arisen; this is to be connected with what was stated previously.
Without walls and devoid of color, yet captivating to the mind; like a painting in a dream or in the sky, it shines forth without action for a long time.

The two occurrences of the word *vā* (or) indicate alternative positions. One perceives a variegated (*citra*) thing seen in a dream; or one perceives a variegated thing seen through delusion in the sky. How is that variegated thing? It is "without a wall" (*abhitti*), meaning devoid of a wall; likewise, it is "devoid of color" (*raṅgarahita*), meaning devoid of colored substances. Furthermore, how is it? It is "without action" (*akarma*), meaning uncreated; likewise, it is "long-lasting and radiant" (*ciraṃ bhāsvara*).
"Radiant for a long time. By these qualifiers, the supramundane nature of the *citra* (the painting) is expressed.

Just as a variegated fire possesses the nature of fire despite being non-fire itself, so too does [the Supreme Being] assume the form and meaning of the word "world," though that world is unreal in its essence.

In that same way, it is likewise. "Consisting of the non-existent" means having a non-existent nature. The term *jagat* (world) refers to the object of the word-form; this is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is emphasized. Thus, one perceives that which possesses the status of being the object of the word-form "world. How so? Just as a painted fire is not fire and lacks the power to burn—it is not fire yet—nevertheless, it possesses and maintains the nature of fire, though that nature is non-existent.
It rose up like a stone leaf rich with a garland of wave-lotuses, appearing like a heap of grime from the powdering of the whirring of the discus.
It is perceived as if rising like a stone-slab (*śilāpattra*) rich with garlands of waves and lotuses.

For on a stone-slab there are lines in the form of waves and in the form of lotuses; these alone are to be understood here as the "garlands of waves and lotuses. And the objects [of cognition] here stand in the place of those garlands of waves and lotuses. Furthermore, how is it perceived? To this, he says:

Regarding the word *cakra*: it refers to a wheel that is being rotated. One perceives what arises as if it were a heap of impurity consisting of the powder of the whirring sound (*śūtkāra*). For indeed, when a wheel is rotated, dust from the ground rises up accompanied by a whirring sound.
Like a forest in summer with withered leaves, fallen and perished, and devoid of sap; resembling a dance distracted by death, yet provoking laughter from the stone statues of women.
It causes laughter like the smile of a stone woman.
The solitary dancing within a house of darkness is the behavior of a madman; [but now] the mist of ignorance has been stilled, like the autumnal sky of pure consciousness.

The intention here is that in a house of darkness, whatever dance of each individual is perceived, it is perceived as being entirely more unreal than [the reality]. Beyond this, with the intention that one perceives that which consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and resides in pure consciousness, he says: "tranquil" (*praśānta*). When this is heard by the listeners in this section on origination, this [world] becomes one where the mist of ignorance has been stilled.
The sky of the autumn of gnosis is realized.
It is as if carved upon a pillar, or painted upon a wall; it is as if fashioned from clay—endowed with consciousness, yet devoid of it.

It is perceived as if carved upon a pillar—that pillar being called pure consciousness (cinmātra). Likewise, it is perceived as if a painting placed upon a wall—that wall being called pure consciousness. Here, "mud" is to be understood as the very nature of pure consciousness; it is "sentient" because its essence is pure consciousness, and "insentient" because it is an object of perception.
Then the fourth section, concerning stability, was composed; it consists of three thousand verses and comprises well-expounded narratives and legends.
The *ākhyāna*s and *ākhyāyikā*s are called "the beautiful" (*śobhana*); it consists of those.
Now, what was said in the section on persistence? To this he replies:
"In this way, the world, having attained the state of persistence in the form of the sense of 'I', is fully developed through the sequence of seer and seen"—this has been described here. (MU 2.17.30)
The sense is that, in this context, the very persistence of the world—which consists of the notion of "I" (ahaṃbhāva)—is for the most part being determined.
"This delusion of the world, resplendent throughout the expanse of the ten directions, has thus come to such growth"—this is what is said there concerning its long duration.
For a long time means for a great duration; that is to say, for the most part.
Then follows the Upaśāntiprakaraṇa, consisting of five thousand [verses]; this fifth section is declared to be purifying and beautiful through the lineage of the sages.
By the lineages of sages who will be mentioned as examples; "sundaram" means beautiful and delightful.
Now, in response to the inquiry "What is being described here?", he says:
"The delusion that 'this world, I, and you' has arisen; this [delusion] is pacified"—this is what is stated in this summary of verses. (MU 2.17.33)

"This world, I, and you—that is he"—such is the delusion that has arisen. While it exists, it is pacified; this is what is explained in this chapter on pacification (*upaśāntiprakaraṇa*). Of what nature is this [chapter]? It is one in which there is a compendium of verses (*śloka-saṅgraha*). In such [a chapter], "he" (*sa*) refers to the reference to the ultimate cause (*paramakāraṇa*).
"Now, what will be accomplished by hearing this? To this he replies:
"When the section on tranquility is heard, the cycle of existence ceases; for that which was clearly perceived through delusion alone is now found to be unattainable."
Of what nature is *saṃsṛti*? It is clearly manifest through delusion alone—that is, through erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) alone. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is that which possesses some slight attainment, perception, or contact (*sparśa*). The implication is that otherwise, the section on *nirvāṇa* would be rendered purposeless.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of transmigratory existence remains thereafter, he says:
"Only a hundredth part remains, consisting of subsided delusion; it resides in the mind of another's volition, like the unreal splendor of a city [in a dream]. (MU 2.17.35)
This is clear.

It is as unobtainable as the roar of a battle in a dream occurring at one's own side, and like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt from a cloud intoxicated by its own volition once it has been stilled.

The delusion of intoxication seen in conceptual construction is the delusion of intoxication that is conceptual construction; that which is the cessation of the delusion of intoxication that is conceptual construction—of that, there is a terrifying sound like a thunderbolt; it is like that.
She is like a city created by the construction of dreams and mental constructs that have been forgotten; she is the dark-limbed maiden who will be the festival of gardens and cities yet to come.

She whose body (aṅga) is like that of the woman named Śyāmā— who was full of festive joy and passion in the future city-garden, and who was like a city comparable to one created by him whose [creation] consists of those two dreams and mental constructs which have been forgotten— she was such as that.

It is like the experience of the meaning of a fierce story being told by a tongue that has vanished; it is like a wall-surface pervaded by a painting residing within the mind, though not drawn upon it.

Furthermore, of what nature was it? It was like that which possesses a comparison with the experience of the meaning of those fierce words being uttered—not by one whose tongue is lost, but not by one whose tongue is destroyed. What is it like?
It is pervaded by those paintings which are both unetched and situated within the mind, as well as those paintings situated within the mind of a painter.
Like the foundation of a wall.
When being thoroughly investigated, it is like a city of imaginary construction; though possessing all seasons, it is unarisen, and its excellent form is not clearly manifest.

Being made to be remembered, yet not having been forgotten; that which is transparent and without walls, a city of imagination—resembling that [city] is its likeness. Like the crushing—that is, the destruction—of the unborn bridegroom by all those who have reached their season (*ṛtumatī*), so too is her form indistinct. The mention of "those who have reached their season" is for the purpose of making known that she has ascended into the intellect by virtue of being in close proximity.
Thus it has been said.
It is colored by the essence of spring through the form of future excellent flowers, and is like a river of gentle water with its surging waves hidden within.

She whose coloring is like that of the essence of spring—which possesses a beautiful form and is destined to be called "Flower" (puṣpa)—that is the meaning. She is one in whom a multitude of waves is submerged within; she is such a river of gentle water, endowed with placid waters. By these qualifiers [she is described].
Immediately following the hearing of the section on the pacification of the cup, it is indicated that creation exists as a nature consisting merely of its appearance to the intellect.
Then the sixth chapter, titled "Nirvāṇa," has been proclaimed; the remaining portion of the text should be known as its extent, which bestows great benefit.
Thereafter, following the section on pacification (upaśāntiprakaraṇa), the remaining portion of the text consists of sixteen thousand five hundred [verses] in extent.
[Objection: But what will be accomplished by hearing that? To this he says:

When that [Self] is realized, the hearer becomes one who has attained Nirvana, with all conceptual constructions stilled; his nature is the light of consciousness which is beyond the object of thought, the essence of pure awareness, free from all affliction. (MU 2.17.42)
He is extinguished, merged into Brahman; he is the conscious self whose nature is pure knowledge; he is free from affliction, being devoid of the malady known as the visible world.

Transparent as the sheath of the supreme ether, with all wandering through existence stilled, he has brought the journey of the world to its conclusion and remains well-established, having accomplished what was to be done.

He by whom the course of the world has been brought to its end—that is, led to its cessation—is such a one. He is "one who has accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakartavya*), meaning one by whom all that was to be performed has been completed. Furthermore, he is "well-established," like a vajra-pillar amidst all the vast undertakings [of the world], resembling the sky; he is fully satiated, having swallowed the entire web of the world exactly as it exists.

The meaning is that among all those extensive undertakings, he is an immovable pillar of diamond (*vajrastambha*). He resembles the sky (*nabhonibha*) because, even by means of actions performed for the sake of maintaining the body, he remains untainted and is thus like space. Having swallowed—that is, having dissolved—the web of the world into his own self, which is the nature of consciousness, he is "extremely satisfied," meaning he is free from all dependence.

Having become like space, with all mental constructions regarding the perception of form entirely vanished, he is abandoned by the states of cause, effect, agency, that which is to be discarded, and that which is to be accepted.
Form is the object; light is the means for its apprehension; mental attention (*manaskṛti*) is *manaskāra*; that is to say, it is the mental coordination of the form apprehended by means of light.
Though possessing a body, he is bodiless; though within saṃsāra, he is beyond saṃsāra. Consisting of pure consciousness, he is like the interior of a stone.
"With body" (sadeha) means that only the sentient being remains because the physical body still persists; "without body" (nirdeha) means the absence of ego-identification with the body.

"Consisting of consciousness" (cinmaya) means having the nature of pure awareness due to the certainty of "I am. That which is the interior of solid stone—that which is its interior—by that he is compared; such is he, because he consists of consciousness that is beyond the reach of thought.

The sun of consciousness, though shining in the world, appears as if it were the interior of darkness; although its nature is that of supreme illumination, it has, as it were, entered into a state of supreme blindness.

The Sun of Consciousness (*cidāditya*) is the very nature of the Sun of Consciousness; for this reason, even while shining in the world, there is indeed no entity whatsoever that is devoid of contact with consciousness, because if it were so, it would follow that such an entity lacks existence. It is like the interior of darkness—that which has a resemblance to the interior of darkness—because it is devoid of the differentiation of objects; for indeed, within the interior of darkness...

There occurs a division of categories: although its nature is that of supreme illumination and its nature is that of the transcendent light of consciousness, it is as if it has fallen into utter blindness, because it does not perceive anything.
The wicked play of saṃsāra has been obstructed; the cholera of desire has been destroyed; the vampire of egoism has perished; he possesses a body, yet is bodiless.
This is clear.
This splendor of the world rests upon a single tip of one of his pores, like a bee upon a flower of Mount Meru.
In some [part] so extremely subtle that it is impossible to describe—in other words, like a dream; for in a dream, the world of the dream exists within a certain part of a person.
Within the hollow of the sky of consciousness in every single atom, it sustains thousands of world-glories and, having created them, beholds them.

Within the hollow—the center—of the sky of consciousness, which is his very own nature, the mere space of pure consciousness; he holds, that is, sustains, thousands of world-glories within every single atom. Not only does he hold them, but because he abides as their witness, he also beholds them.
"Now, how is it that he contains thousands of world-glories within himself? To this, he says in a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O Great-minded One, even by hundreds of thousands of Lakṣas of Hari, Hara, and Abja, the expansion of the heart of one who possesses liberation cannot be measured; alas, there is certainly no such expansion for that which is non-substantial. (MU 2.17.51)

"Bata" expresses certainty. O Mahāmati! For a person possessed of liberation—one who is endowed with liberation by way of hearing the section on Nirvāṇa—the heart becomes "pravitata. This is an expression where the state (*bhāva*) is emphasized; thus, the meaning is that the heart is "widely expanded.
That [expansion] cannot be reached by even hundreds of thousands of Hari, Hara, or Aja (Brahmā) through the domain of measurement or weighing, because it is not a substantial entity (*avastu*).
The extensive multitude of entities consisting of forms such as Hari, Hara, and Abja—which are in fact non-entities (avastu)—surely does not exist; "nūnam" signifies certainty.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a non-entity to attain the status of a real entity (vastu). Thus, the implication is that the aforementioned undesirable consequence regarding location does not arise. May there be auspiciousness! MT_2,17.51 //
Thus ends the seventeenth canto in the Mumukṣu-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. For the sake of engaging the listeners, he explains that this treatise, being distinct from others, serves as a means for others to attain right knowledge:
"Upon merely reading this, supreme awakening arises, because from the seed once sown, the excellent fruit necessarily follows. (MU 2.18.1)

In this compendium which sets forth the means to liberation, what is awakening? From that awakening, the auspicious fruit known as liberation—the true fruit—inevitably comes to be. Like what? Like [the fruit] from a sown seed.

Now, one might ask: "Why should I abandon other treatises composed by the Great Sage and accept this very treatise alone? To this, he replies: "Even a human-authored treatise is to be accepted if it reveals logical reasoning; however, another, even if authored by a Ṛṣi, must be rejected. One who relies solely on logic should cultivate this [attitude]. (MU 2.18.2)

"Pauruṣa" means composed by a human being; it is "ādeya," meaning it should be accepted, as it provides understanding through reasoning and provides understanding through sound logic (*sattarka*). Any other [type of scripture] does not provide such understanding through reasoning. "Ārṣa" means composed by a *ṛṣi*. In this regard, those endowed with intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) should understand a certain underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), which we have indicated at the very outset: that for those possessed of insight, [the meaning] is to be known by themselves, whereas for those devoid of it, it cannot be fully expressed.
Thus it has been said.
A statement that is endowed with reason is to be accepted even from a child; anything else, even if spoken by the Lotus-born One, is to be rejected like a blade of grass.

In this case as well, those possessed of discernment (*pratibhāvat*) should personally understand for themselves the meaning stated at the outset as something to be known by oneself; nor should they show disregard for this treatise because of their understanding of it, for that would result in the loss of their discernment. Likewise, in subsequent instances as well, one should infer for oneself wherever appropriate.
Furthermore, he explains this very point in another way:
"Who would instruct that passionate man who, having abandoned the Ganges standing right before him, drinks bitter well-water, thinking, 'This is my father's well'?"

Who would instruct— that is, advise— a man who, having abandoned the water of the Ganges standing before him, drinks the bitter water of a well for the sake of thinking, "This well belongs to my own father"? The meaning is that such an attached person, possessed of the defect known as attachment toward his father, is not worthy of instruction.

This is the intended meaning here: that person who rejects even a human statement endowed with sound reasoning on the grounds that "this is of human origin," yet accepts a statement of a seer (*ārṣa*) even though it lacks such reasoning merely because it is "of a seer"— for such a person, no instruction should be given.
He follows the very subject at hand:
"Just as when dawn has broken, light will necessarily arrive; so too, upon this being merely recited, one's own discernment will arrive."
The feminine form "uṣasī" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage; "svavivekaḥ" means self-discrimination (*ātmaviveka*).

When [the teaching] has been heard from the mouth of a wise person or understood by oneself, and when a mental impression (saṃskāra) has gradually arisen in the intellect through repeated investigation; //MU_2,18.6//
First, there arises within him a highly refined command of speech—pure, liberated, and lofty like a climbing vine—which serves as the ornament for the assembly hall.
This is clear.

"Surely, for me who am dispassionate, what is the purpose of refined speech? To this he replies: "A supreme dispassion arises, endowed with the quality of greatness, by which even kings and even pythons are moved to affection."
For even kings, when they are detached, develop affection for those who are like pythons.
A person who knows what precedes and what follows becomes wise in all matters, just as one with good eyesight and a lamp in hand perceives objects clearly at night.
In all respects, in all worldly transactions.
The defects such as greed and delusion gradually diminish sufficiently, just as the mists in the directions fade away when autumn is near.

What are greed, delusion, and the rest? The meaning is that they become attenuated, just as mists in a direction where autumn is near—that is, in a direction approaching the autumn season—become thin.
The intellects require only the practice of discernment; no action whatsoever bears fruit without its own repeated practice.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose do they require the practice of discrimination? To this, he says: "Not anything whatsoever... (na kācana).
The mind attains clarity like a great lake in autumn; it achieves supreme equanimity like the ocean when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.

Clarity (*prasāda*) is purity due to being free from the stains of passion and other defilements; it is supreme (*param*), meaning unsurpassed; and it bestows—that is, sustains—the quality called equanimity (*sāmya*). Here too, the mind alone is the agent.
With its darkness dispelled, like a diamond-pointed flame that has extinguished the veil of gloom, wisdom (*prajñā*) blazes forth intensely, discerning the true nature of all things.
"Nirasta" means gone far away; "kālimā" means turbidity; she is one who possesses that [turbidity].
Views such as those of wretchedness, poverty, and fault, though their inner nature has been revealed, do not cut into one's vital points, just as arrows do not pierce one who is clad in armor.
"Shown" means analyzed. "Those whose internal portion"—that is, the inner part called the core—is [present], means they are known to be without essence. //MT_2,18.14//
The terrifying fears of cyclic existence do not tear at the heart of the wise man, even when they stand before him, just as rats cannot gnaw through a great boulder.
Of what nature is the heart? Even though it stands before one, even though it is situated in front; furthermore, of what nature is it? It is wise.
"How can there be primacy for either destiny or human effort regarding birth and action?"—such a multitude of doubts subsides just as darkness vanishes in the day.
Between destiny and human effort—that is, between fate and personal exertion—destiny is the primary cause.
In every way, attachment to all things subsides when the light of wisdom has arisen, just as it does when the night has passed.

In all things—whether they be fit for renunciation or acquisition—in every object whatsoever, attachment in the form of giving and taking ceases entirely. Under what condition? When the light of the vow has arrived. At what time? As if when the night has passed. The sense is that equanimity alone prevails everywhere.
Like the ocean, there is profundity; like Mount Meru, there is stability; and like the moon, inner coolness arises for the one who investigates.
This is clear.
That state of liberation while living gradually reaches its full fruition for that yogi who has stilled all mental constructs, having entered into it.
She is well-known; "having entered" means having effected possession.
Cool toward all objects, pure, supremely illuminating, and wise, it attains supreme radiance like the full moonlight of the moon.
In all objects—whether possessed of existence or non-existence, and in all categories of things—that [intellect] is cool, being free from the distress known as joy and resentment;

it is pure, being devoid of passion and the like; and it is such that it bestows the supreme light, which is the light of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). This beautiful intellect is "Sudhī"; it is "Aindavī," pertaining to the moon.
When the sun of discernment shines in the stainless sky of the heart, illuminating with the light of tranquility,
the banners of strife— the makers of the caravan of misfortune— do not arise.

In one who possesses tranquility as their very light, the banners of *kali*—that is, the signs of strife and agitation, such as the defects of passion and the like—do not arise; rather, they subside. Just as at sunrise the comets known as *dhūmaketavas* do not rise, but instead become calm, pure, gentle, and remain fixed in their high positions, so too do cravings—which are otherwise unsteady and dull—become like rows of clouds in autumn.
They are neither restless nor dull; they are not restless and dull.
Vulgar cruelty, which performs every kind of base act, ceases like the wretched sport of ghosts at the arrival of day; its face becomes dejected.
One who acts at random is one who acts improperly; for through vulgarity, a man does indeed whatever comes to hand.
Mental anxieties do not destroy the intellect that is firmly fixed upon the foundation of Dharma and has ascended the yoke of fortitude, just as winds cannot uproot a painted creeper.

Dharma alone is the wall; she was clinging to it, and for that very reason had ascended the burden of fortitude—that is to say, she was endowed with steadfastness. For one who is joined with Dharma becomes firm (dhīra). She was a creeper of variegated form—a "citra-latā"—that very one.
A living being does not fall into the pit that consists of attachment to sense objects; for who indeed, once the path of knowledge is known, would run headlong into a chasm?

[The compound] *viṣayāsaṅgarūpiṇi* means "consisting of attachment to sense objects" or "consisting of addiction to enjoyments. He supports this very point with the second half of the verse: "Who indeed... (kaḥ kila).

The intellect of the wise man delights in action that is consistent with true scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous, as it arises according to its own nature, just as a noble woman finds pleasure in the courtyard of the inner apartments.

Those whose conduct is virtuous through immersion in the true scripture known as the means to liberation—for such people [this occurs] according to what has been attained, coming by way of natural flow, and not without effort.
Within each and every one of the atoms that exist throughout the millions of worlds, he whose mind is free from the notion of creation beholds the worlds situated therein.

He is one whose intellect is free from the notion of creation. It is a marvel that there is a perception of creation within every single atom. Through the knowledge of the pervasion of pure consciousness—which is the seed of creation—one should understand the perception of creation within every single atom.
For a person whose inner organ has been purified by the realization of the means to liberation, the flood of enjoyments neither causes distress nor brings delight at any time.
The meaning is that he cultivates only equanimity toward enjoyments.
He beholds those multitudes of creations falling and rising without restraint in every single atom, like waves upon the water.
They fall and become latent; they leap up and manifest.
He feels no aversion toward things that have arisen, nor does he long for those that have ceased; though awakened, he performs his duties like a tree that is not yet awake.
Its state of non-awakening should be understood as the lack of awakening within itself regarding saṃsāra.
"Now, what kind of excellence would he possess? To this, he says:
"He is seen to be like the common world, following whatever comes to him; yet, in the attainment of desired or undesired results, his heart is not defeated. (MU 2.18.31)

He is common to the world and not possessed of any excellence; he follows what has been obtained as it comes in the natural flow. He who possesses such conformity to what is obtained is "one who conforms to what is obtained. In his heart—that is, in his mind—he is not defeated, meaning he is not overcome by joy or resentment.
Having studied and analyzed this entire treatise, one indeed experiences this for oneself; it is not merely a matter of words like a boon or a curse.

"You must indeed experience this aforementioned result. To address the expectation—"But how can we be capable of experiencing this due to the fear of transgression (pratyavāya)?"—he says: "But it is not said [to be like that]," with the words "like mantras and so forth" being the ellipsis.

[Objection: "But how can we engage with this which is so difficult to understand? To this, the author says: "This treatise is indeed easy to understand; it is a beautiful poem adorned with various ornaments, dense with aesthetic flavor (rasa), and instructive through its illustrative examples. (MU 2.18.33)
The phrase "established by means of examples" is a reason expressed through a qualification [of the subject] for the sake of easy understanding.
One who knows even a little of the words and their meanings understands this by himself; however, he who does not know this by himself must hear it from a learned man.
He awakens; that is, he knows. [Objection: But for one who lacks knowledge of words and their meanings, what is to be done? To this, he says: "by himself."
[Objection: "But what will be accomplished by hearing this? To this, he says:
"When this has been heard, reflected upon, and known, then for the attainment of liberation, no other practice such as austerity, meditation, or recitation is of any further use here. (MU 2.18.35)

When it has been heard, brought within the range of hearing; when it has been reflected upon, brought within the range of reflection; and when it has been known, firmly established—then for one who has thus engaged in hearing and the other stages [of practice].
Indeed, for a person who has repeatedly examined this treatise through intense study, preceded by scholarship and preceded by the purification of the mind; MU_2,18.36.
The mature conviction "I am the world"—this demon of the seer and the seen—subsides of its own accord and without obstacle, just as a ghost vanishes at the rising of the sun.
By this, it has been stated that both the external purpose and the internal purpose will be accomplished.
The delusion that "the world exists" and "I exist" subsides even while it persists; like a dream-delusion once fully recognized, it no longer delights one at all.
It remains just as it is; it has not entered into a state of internal absorption through the application of mantras and so forth. [Objection: But how can there be pacification of that which remains?

To this he says: "the delusion of a dream. The meaning is that even for one who remains in a state of indifference (*arasa*), pacification is indeed to be understood, because there is an absence of anything that causes agitation.

Just as the joy or sorrow of a person regarding a city of their imagination does not cause them distress, so too the delusion of the world does not afflict one who has fully realized its nature within.
When [the truth] is fully understood and correctly ascertained within the mind, joy and dejection do not afflict one; this is what is conveyed by the word "tathā" (thus).
Just as a painted snake, once fully recognized, does not cause fear of a snake, so too the perceived snake, once fully recognized, does not bestow pleasure or pain.
"This variegated snake has been fully understood" means it has been correctly determined; the "snake called the visible" refers to the snake that is perceived as visible.
Just as the snake-nature of a painted snake perishes through thorough knowledge, so too does saṃsāra, though it remains as it is, become pacified.
This is clear.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the attainment of the ultimate truth is exceedingly difficult for us? And thus, it is indeed improper to immerse oneself in this treatise for the sake of attaining it? To this, he says:
"In the touching of the sprout of the *sumana* flower, there may be some degree of contact; but in the attainment of the state of the ultimate truth, there is no contact for us. (MU 2.18.42)

"Sumanaḥpallavāmarśe" means in the crushing of flower-buds; "vyatikaraḥ" means effort; "naḥ" refers to us who know what is logical; the meaning is that this applies to us who know what is logical, but not to you who do not know what is logical.
He explains the very absence of such a conflict:

"In the crushing of a flower petal, there occurs a vibration of its parts; however, in this case [of cognition], there is only the awareness of the mere intellect, not the awareness of the limbs or their parts."

It goes; it becomes engaged. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *gam* (to go) is used here in this sense. Of the limbs—that is, the members of the body. "Awakening" means setting in motion.
Seated on a comfortable seat, eating as much as is appropriate, and never remaining engaged in activities contrary to right conduct, one should enjoy the web of worldly enjoyments.
One should contemplate this treatise, as well as other subjects, with ease, according to the opportunity, according to the place, and according to the possibility of association with the virtuous.
One attains the awakening of great wisdom, which brings peace to saṃsāra, by means of which one no longer undergoes the crushing of the machine of rebirth.

"According to possibility" means not achieved through forced effort; for one who persists in actions contrary to right conduct (*sadācāra*), a fault consisting of the tendency to reject or adopt [what is improper] arises, and thus it is said "one should not persist. "At every moment" means at each instant. "Pleasant" means that which bestows happiness.
"Where there is association with the virtuous according to possibility": this is the treatise (*śāstra*) to be spoken by me, known as the "Means to Liberation" (*mokṣopāya*).
"Other" refers to another scripture similar to this one. "Great knowledge-awareness" (*mahājñānabodha*) is awareness whose nature is great knowledge.
This [term] is connected with the first half of the verse.
Those beings who, having obtained enjoyments, remain attached to their taste—those lowest of men are not even worth mentioning, for they are like worms in their own mother’s excrement.
In this much, in this limited amount of rasa, there are beings, that is, common creatures.
Having thus described the greatness of the scripture, he addresses Śrī Rāma:
"Listen now, O Rāghava, to this expansion of knowledge—the very essence of the heart—being told by me."
That whose internal state is more essential than the intellect; the meaning is that it transcends the intellect.
